For these states, the one-particle approximation overestimates the mean dip depth by about 16-18% on 24 sites and underestimates it by 33-56% in the 6,144-site sample. Extrapolating from 24 sites would therefore give the wrong sign for this correction on those four larger tori under the same disorder prescription.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

papers.title: ViewPACT: Multi-View Geometric Augmentation and Pose-Action Co-Training for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
papers.abstract: Image policies are scalable but remain brittle to camera viewpoint changes. On LIBERO, we identify proprioception as an input shortcut: masking robot states sharply degrades several policies, while retraining from images alone recovers much of the loss. We introduce ViewPACT, an image policy trained with privileged geometric supervision. Auxiliary objectives recover end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame, while deployment requires only RGB observations. Joint geometric supervision improves mean simulation success from 37.4% to 78.4% under unseen external-camera viewpoints, with more modest gains under separately evaluated object, scene, and camera-intrinsic shifts. Across four real-robot tasks, combining simulated and real-image geometric supervision achieves 68.1% mean success, versus 3.1% for fixed-view behavior cloning and 30.6% for the strongest evaluated alternative. These results support geometric supervision for viewpoint robustness in the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.

papers.title: HiPerfCC-StateReuse: Ciphertext Reuse for Fast Confidential GPU Data Movement
papers.abstract: Confidential GPUs offer near-native on-device compute performance, but transfers between CPU and GPU TEEs through untrusted host memory require bulk CPU encryption and decryption, even for unchanged data. Existing software techniques overlap or parallelize these operations but retain their per-byte CPU cost. Reusing exported ciphertext could avoid this work, but GPU TEE firmware enforces direction-specific encryption keys and fresh per-transfer initialization vectors (IVs), preventing direct reuse. We introduce ciphertext rebinding, a purely software primitive enabling repeated and cross-GPU ciphertext reuse on existing GPU TEEs without hardware changes, while preserving confidentiality, integrity, and freshness. Specifically, ciphertext rebinding exploits the separation between ciphertext-dependent and IV-dependent components in GPU TEE's AES-GCM authentication: a GPU-precomputed summary under the destination key can enable the CPU to update authentication tags without processing the payload. With this modification, GPU's subsequent read on the retained ciphertext can still proceed through the GPU's hardware-fixed copy-engine interfaces, which cannot be modified by software. An additional GPU correction step can then compensate for differences in the keys and IVs to recover the original plaintext. By retaining GPU-exported ciphertext in untrusted host memory, ciphertext rebinding avoids bulk CPU decryption and re-encryption, improving effective bandwidth for GPU-state restoration and sharing. We implement this primitive in HiPerfCC-StateReuse through only driver and library changes, combining batched submissions with pipelined GPU processing and copy-engine transfers. We evaluate transfer efficiency and CPU overhead through microbenchmarks, and application performance through three case studies: model switching, key-value cache offloading, and cross-instance cache sharing.

papers.title: RES: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models with Rolling Entropy Sampling
papers.abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.

papers.title: Plane Curves Whose Curvature Is a Function of the Distance to the Tangent Line: Relations Between Karpenkov's Areal and Angular Densities
papers.abstract: For a plane curve and a point $O$, O. Karpenkov introduced the areal density $A$ and the angular density $B$ as smooth counterparts of the alternating entries of an LLS sequence. Here $A$ is the signed distance from $O$ to the tangent line, and, with the order of the chords in the signed definition fixed here, $A^2B=\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the signed curvature. A relation between the two densities therefore prescribes the curvature as a function of the distance to the tangent line. Karpenkov asked which curves have $AB$, or $B$ alone, constant. The equation $AB=C$ gives the shrinking, stationary and expanding profiles of planar curve shortening. For constant nonzero $B$, choose the orientation so that $B>0$. Curves with positive support have periodic support or are centred circles. The noncircular closed curves are classified by their turning fractions in $(1/2,1/\sqrt3)$; the centred circle is the only embedded closed solution. Negative support gives smooth open graphs whose two ends approach rays from the origin. On positive support the polar reciprocal is a constant-force orbit, and the original curve is a rotated and scaled velocity curve of that orbit. For $A^3B=C$ we determine which ends extend to infinity, reach a cusp, or spiral into the origin. We describe regularity and the range of turning fractions for the positive-support family $A^pB=C$. Finally, for a general relation $B=\Phi(A)$ the polar reciprocal is an orbit of the central force $L^2/\Phi(1/r)$; we describe the ends of all arcs with $AB<0$ and show that a closed curve with turning fraction $m/n$ has exactly $n(m-1)$ double points. We also describe the curves whose areal or angular density is a linear function of the arclength.

papers.title: Single-Transformer Latent Diffusion
papers.abstract: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes (~60M, ~115M, and ~215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.

papers.title: Strong holonomicity of functions on curves
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a smooth affine irreducible curve over $\mathbb C$, and let ${\mathcal D} = {\mathcal D} (X)$ be the ring of global differential operators on $X$. To every nonzero operator $L \in {\mathcal D} $ we attach a non-negative integer $n(L)$, the holonomicity index of $L$, which is defined in an elementary way, by counting solutions of $L$ in the truncated local rings at the singular points of $L$. Our main theorem shows that $n(L)$ coincides with the Calogero--Moser index of the Weyl closure ${\rm cl}(L) = {\mathcal D}(K) \cap {\mathcal D} $ of $L$, i.e. with the integer $n$ labelling the Calogero--Moser space $ {\mathcal C}_n(X,\mathcal{I})$ that contains the isomorphism class of the left ideal ${\rm cl}(L)$ under the classification of ideals of ${\mathcal D}$ given in [Berest--Chalykh, 2012]. The proof is based on a dual version of the Cannings--Holland correspondence, which describes left ideals of ${\mathcal D}$ in terms of finite-dimensional spaces of algebraic distributions on $X$, and an explicit formula for the Calogero--Moser index given in terms of these distributions. We apply these results to annihilators of locally holomorphic functions on $X$: we call a holonomic function $f$ strongly holonomic if the Calogero--Moser index of ${\rm Ann}_{\mathcal D}(f)$ is positive, and we compute this index in a number of interesting cases.

papers.title: HyperHarness: Learning to Generate Personalized Agent Harnesses from User Histories
papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents rely on an agent harness, the surrounding memory and control code, to connect user history with downstream decisions. Existing methods typically employ either a single shared memory workflow across all users, which is efficient to deploy but cannot adapt how evidence is retrieved and interpreted across diverse histories, or per-user harness optimization, which customizes behavior for each user but requires costly repeated candidate evaluation at deployment and suffers from sparse, noisy supervision in raw logs. To address this trade-off, we present HyperHarness, a framework that learns a shared history-to-harness generator to synthesize executable, user-specific retrieval and answer-guidance code directly from user histories. Given a user's permitted history, HyperHarness prompts a construction LLM to write personalized retrieval and guidance functions, while downstream task scores across training users supervise iterative refinements to the shared generator without reference harnesses or answering-model updates. At deployment, the frozen generator constructs a harness for each unseen user in a single pass from history alone, eliminating per-user task-scored search. Across three benchmarks (PersonaMemv3, Mem-PAL, and MemoryCD) and three answering models (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, and GPT-5.6-Luna), HyperHarness achieves the highest aggregate score in seven of nine settings and ranks second in the remaining two, improving over the strongest baselines by up to 5.95 points while cutting matched answer-time tokens by 90.32% over long-context prompting. Analyses show that optimization tailors context allocation to each executor, transfers to unseen user clusters, and amortizes adaptation costs.

papers.title: A Simple Optimal Algorithm for Directed Multi-Failure Replacement Paths
papers.abstract: Given a graph $G = (V, E)$ and two vertices $s, t \in V$, the $f$-fault replacement paths ($f$-FRP) problem asks to compute, for every set $F$ of at most $f$ edges, the distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G \setminus F$. In this paper, we present a $3$-FRP algorithm in deterministic $O(n^3 \log n)$ time for directed weighted graphs. We also present a deterministic $O(n^4)$ time algorithm for $4$-FRP in directed weighted graphs, which implies a deterministic $O(n^f)$ time algorithm for $f$-FRP for every $f \ge 4$. Since the output size of $f$-FRP can be $\Theta(n^f)$, our algorithms are optimal for every $f \ge 4$ and nearly optimal for $f = 3$. Our algorithms also extend to the single-source and all-pairs settings with $f-1$ and $f-2$ failures, respectively, with the same time complexity as $f$-FRP. Moreover, our algorithms are remarkably simple.

papers.title: Exact stress-tensor fluctuations from conformal symmetry and black hole radiation
papers.abstract: Semiclassical gravity is sourced by the expectation value of the stress tensor, and it is reliable only if the fluctuations around this value are small. In two dimensions, conformal symmetry captures the essential physics of Hawking radiation in its s-wave sector and determines the mean value exactly, for any background and any quantum state. We show that it also determines the local fluctuations of the null components $T_{\pm\pm}$. The square of the stress tensor is defined by the operator product expansion, up to a multiple $\alpha$ of $\partial_\pm^2T_{\pm\pm}$ that labels point-splitting prescriptions. Its transformation law under the conformal map to locally inertial coordinates gives the variance in closed form. The relative fluctuation scales as $1/c$, with $c$ the central charge. For the Schwarzschild black hole it is $22/5c$ for the Hawking flux at infinity, that of flat-space thermal radiation. At the horizon it is $-44\alpha/3c$ for the outgoing flux and $(238+720\alpha)/5c$ for the ingoing flux that drives the backreaction. Both reduce to $22/5c$ for $\alpha=-3/10$, which corresponds to the M\"obius-covariant prescription. For large $c$ these results support the semiclassical approximation.

papers.title: Recurrent Point Transformer via Test-Time Training
papers.abstract: Real-world point clouds are not naturally bounded: 3D scans grow as sensors move through rooms, LiDAR surveys extend across forest plots, and 4D captures can span thousands of frames. Yet most point-cloud encoders are designed for fixed-size inputs, forcing inference-time cropping or tiling that loses long-range context and requires ad-hoc output stitching. We formulate arbitrary-extent point-cloud segmentation as recurrent sequence-of-chunks processing and introduce PoinTTT, a recurrent point-cloud encoder built on Point Transformer V3 (PTv3). PoinTTT augments PTv3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training (LaCT) layers in both the encoder and decoder. Each LaCT layer maintains compact fast weights as recurrent state: tokens from each chunk update the fast weights, which are then applied to produce chunk features and passed to the next chunk. This design allows PoinTTT to train on fixed-size chunks while processing scenes of arbitrary spatial or temporal extent, with activation memory bounded by the chunk size. A pilot study on ScanNet and nuScenes shows that recurrent TTT improves segmentation over PTv3 baselines. On FOR-instanceV2, PoinTTT achieves state-of-the-art forest semantic segmentation of 87.9 mIoU with nearly constant memory. On HOI4D, online full-sequence recurrent inference carries state across clips rather than resetting at benchmark boundaries, reaching 42.6 mIoU; a matched full-sequence Mamba control reaches approximately 39.9. These results suggest that test-time training is a practical primitive for scalable spatial and temporal point-cloud understanding.

papers.title: Sub-Gaussian HDLSS Principal Component Analysis: High-Probability Theory and Numerical Evidence for NRM, CDM, and Block Noise Reduction
papers.abstract: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a finite-rank score matrix, an isotropic bulk shift, and a high-probability remainder governed by the bulk trace \tau_0, Frobenius scale q_0, and largest noise eigenvalue b_0 = ||\Lambda_0||_{op}. This decomposition separates fixed-score HDLSS limits from joint limits in which n also grows. It shows that sequential noise reduction generally targets a score oracle containing a later-spike subtraction, while an oracle block correction avoids that subtraction when the signal rank is known. A parallel cross-data-matrix bound explains the benefit and cost of sample splitting. Reproducible Gaussian-factor simulations with 1,000 replications per configuration confirm the score-oracle approximation, the multi-spike subtraction, the separation between eigenvalue and eigenvector scales, and the population transition when n grows.

papers.title: DiRGeo: Learning Directional Geometry of Visual Representations
papers.abstract: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.

papers.title: Note on OpenAI's proof of the base of Lagrangian fibrations
papers.abstract: OpenAI proved that every Lagrangian fibration of a compact hyper-K\"ahler manifold has a base $\mathbb P^n$. This expository note summarizes the last section of their paper.

papers.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
papers.abstract: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

papers.title: The Schwarzschild Ringdown Time Prescription on Critical Kerr Plunges
papers.abstract: For a Schwarzschild plunge, constant-amplitude quasinormal-mode convergence has been tied to the source's advanced time at $r=0$, lying $9.435M$ after the $(2,2)$ strain peak. On real prograde critical Kerr plunges, $P(r_-)<0$ forces the ingoing time $v$ to diverge logarithmically at the inner horizon while $u_K$ stays finite. Matching $v$ to $-u_K$ at the unique interior zero $P(r_0)=0$ yields a parameter-free onset hierarchy $(u_{\rm H},u_{r_0},u_{\rm C})$ that recovers $9.435M$ as $a\to 0$ and predicts two-stage residual decay and frequency locking at $(6.85M,11.35M,13.35M)$ on an $a/M=0.9$ eccentric plunge.

papers.title: Fractal dimension of velocity-driven mixing: Reanalysis of Cao et al. (Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)) and the universality of the Marstrand co-dimension rule
papers.abstract: Cao et al. [Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)] compared box-counting fractal dimensions of interfaces from continuum (SOLA-VOF) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of zero-Atwood-number mixing driven by random velocity perturbations. They reported D ~ 1.1-1.4 across physical models. We revisit their results with grid-converged geometric VOF simulations and modern box-counting algorithms. The grid-converged continuum dimension depends on the initial-condition realization (D = 1.13-1.38). Independent LAMMPS simulations show that Cao's MD dimension measures thermal scatter of atomic positions, not interface geometry, because their box-counting window lies below the scale of the interface structure: a flat interface at t=0 gives the same D ~ 1.36. When the thermal scatter is filtered by reducing the midpoint cloud to a curve (median binning at 2 sigma), the MD trajectory converges to the same late-time D ~ 1.43 as the continuum, recovering cross-model universality. We prove that the linear-regime box-counting dimension is exactly D = 2 - beta (A > 0) and D = 5/2 - beta (A = 0), where beta is the spectral exponent of the initial perturbation. For white noise (beta = 0) neither formula applies; Cao's early-time D ~ 2 is a boundary artifact. A three-dimensional grid convergence study gives D_3D = 2.361 +/- 0.002 at 400x400x200. Marstrand's co-dimension rule D_3D = D_2D + 1 shows a 7% discrepancy reflecting IC-realization dependence at A = 0, unlike the buoyancy-driven case where the discrepancy falls with resolution.

papers.title: Quasinormal Modes and Excitation Factors of a Parity-Symmetric Beyond-Horndeski Black Hole
papers.abstract: We study scalar, electromagnetic, and Dirac perturbations of an asymptotically flat black hole in parity-symmetric beyond-Horndeski gravity. The quasinormal spectrum is computed with very-high-order WKB expansions and Pad\'e resummation, with Ces\`aro means used to diagnose internal convergence. The dominant modes are independently tested by time-domain evolution with Prony extraction and by Chebyshev pseudospectral collocation; the latter also provides systematic frequency scans in both the metric-scale and physical ADM-mass normalizations. Excitation factors are obtained separately from Green-function residues by complex-contour integration. In the fixed metric-scale normalization, approaching Schwarzschild generally increases both the oscillation frequency and damping rate, whereas stronger deformation shifts the modes toward lower frequencies and weaker damping. In ADM-mass units, the mildly deformed solutions remain close to Schwarzschild, while the most deformed sector becomes enhanced and nonmonotonic because the asymptotic mass itself varies strongly. The independent methods agree very well, however the sixth-order WKB approximation used in [G. Antoniou, T. D. Pappas, P. Kanti, Phys. Rev. D 112, 084013 (2025)] is insufficient in certain regions of the parameter space: the fundamental-mode discrepancy reaches nine percent in the damping rate and the first-overtone discrepancy can be of order unity. The Schwarzschild excitation factors are recovered. In the strongly deformed regime, their magnitudes can differ from the Schwarzschild values by more than two orders of magnitude in the asymptotic tortoise-coordinate convention. We show that this large effect is predominantly due to the deformation-dependent displacement of the potential barrier in the tortoise coordinate: when its maximum is used as the origin, the excitation factors exhibit much more modest deviations.

papers.title: High-Resolution 3D Micro-CT Database of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Coils for More Accurate Modelling, Technology Benchmarking, and Progress in Coil Design
papers.abstract: Accurate modelling of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coils requires coil-specific geometric and electrical parameters. Yet detailed manufacturer models are rarely available, and internals may be widely available to companies in the field but not to researchers. The development of new coils should ideally build on all existing prior art. This work presents a technology benchmark and modelling-ready dataset for seventeen widely used commercial TMS coils across multiple manufacturers and geometries. High-resolution micro-CT (0.0495 mm resolution, material and density contrast) serves to reconstruct winding and casing structures and to extract parameters directly usable in numerical models, including loop dimensions, conductor cross-section, turn count, winding height, and winding-to-surface (casing) thickness. Complementary electrical measurements provide spectral impedance (series resistance and inductance) scans from 20 Hz to 200 kHz, together with dc resistance. In addition to baseline geometry and impedance, the study documents practical construction features relevant to safety and usability with detailed insights into their internal construction (e.g., cooling architectures and embedded sensing). The resulting benchmark dataset supports coil-specific electric-field simulations, reduces modelling uncertainty associated with generic assumptions (e.g., fixed coil-scalp spacing), and provides a quantitative reference for designing and evaluating new coil technologies against established commercial solutions. As a simulation-readiness example, we generated a calibrated CT-derived MCB70 line-current model for SimNIBS and evaluated its effect on predicted electric-field metrics. Compared with the SimNIBS MCB70 model, the CT-derived model produced measurable differences under identical placement conditions. We provide the dataset online.

papers.title: Certified Comparative Statics for Conservation-Law Equilibrium Layers, with an Application to RNA Interference
papers.abstract: Implicit and equilibrium neural layers define their output as the fixed point of a map. Existing theory certifies that this fixed point exists; it does not certify how it responds to its inputs. For a conservation-law layer with order-preserving coupling we give a form-independent answer: every input-output comparative static is sign-certified if and only if the residual Jacobian is a nonsingular M-matrix, and the certified sign depends only on the sign of the occupancy derivative, so one guarantee covers Langmuir, Hill, and saturating-exponential occupancies. The M-matrix machinery is classical; the contribution is form-independence as the portable invariant, the first certified-sign sensitivity result for a layer of this class, and a sharp phase boundary at which certification is lost while the equilibrium remains well posed. Three consequences follow: the phase boundary, which is strictly stronger than the M-matrix condition; competitive derepression, whose derivative is identically zero for any independent per-target scorer and provably nonzero here; and non-submodularity of resource-coupled suppression. We instantiate on siRNA off-target competition and validate on real public data only, across seventeen microRNAs, two titration studies, and a paired chemical-modification experiment; a second, non-biological instantiation shows the same certified sign on measured physical data. As a trainable layer the operator learns end-to-end while remaining certified-monotone by construction, reaching magnitude parity with a parameter-matched feedforward baseline while expressing a competition effect that baseline cannot represent for any weights. The single-pool instantiation validates the mechanism but does not rank off-target magnitude or resolve position-specific design. Code: https://github.com/shadi97kh/certified-equilibrium-layers

papers.title: A bound for Stieltjes constants of the Riemann zeta function
papers.abstract: The coefficients appearing in the Laurent expansion of the Riemann zeta function are known as the Stieltjes constants and are denoted by $\gamma_n$. Several authors, including Berndt, Matsuoka, Williams and Zhang, and Saad Eddin, have investigated upper bounds for $|\gamma_n|$, with the best known result due to Pauli and Saidak \cite{MR4671618}. In 2003, based on numerical evidence, Kreminski \cite{MR1972742} conjectured that Matsuoka's bound \cite{MR827790} could be considerably improved. Motivated by this conjecture, we employ the saddle-point method to derive an asymptotic formula for the Stieltjes constants, with the saddle point expressed explicitly in terms of the Lambert $W$-function. The resulting formula yields an asymptotic upper bound of the correct order of magnitude. Moreover, the resulting bound is consistent with the conjecture of Farr, Pauli, and Saidak \cite{MR4280128}.

papers.title: On the performance of the randomized Euler scheme for nonlinear ODEs under inexact information
papers.abstract: We analyze the randomized explicit Euler scheme for nonlinear ordinary differential equations under a local one-sided Lipschitz condition, local H\"older regularity in the space variable, and H\"older regularity in the time variable. We allow for noisy evaluations of the right-hand side. For the resulting approximation, we derive an error bound in which the contribution associated with the H\"older regularity in the time variable exhibits the characteristic 1/2-order gain of randomized methods. While existing results cover deterministic schemes under the one-sided Lipschitz condition and randomized schemes under the classical Lipschitz condition, our results combine randomized approximation and one-sided Lipschitz regularity.

papers.title: Linear and non-linear integro-differential equations with variable coefficients and Sonin kernels
papers.abstract: We study linear and non-linear integro-differential equations, with Sonin and absolutely continuous kernels, and with variable coefficients which are either integrable or continuous functions. In the linear case, for all cases, the unique solution is given explicitly by a convergent infinite series involving compositions of convolutions of the kernels and the variable coefficients. Many examples are provided. For the non-linear case, the existence and uniqueness are established under a suitable condition in the non-linear term. The analytic solution is given by the limit of the iterative sequence found from the method of successive approximations. The exact analytical expressions for several problems are found by computing the iterative sequences that approximate the solution.

papers.title: Compact and Long-Term Stable Polarization Entangled Photon-Pair Source
papers.abstract: We present a robust, compact polarization-entangled photon-pair source based on bulk optics that achieves long-term stability, a spectral pair generation rate of $4.24 \times 10^6$ pairs s$^{-1}$ mW$^{-1}$ nm$^{-1}$ constant for pump powers up to 700 mW, an intrinsic heralding efficiency of 59.8% , and a polarization contrast visibility of 99.6%. The source is mechanically designed for vibrational robustness, employing an engineered base plate and a reduced optical layout for less alignment sensitivity and complexity. It operates at telecom wavelengths in C-band with a typical type-0 SPDC spectral output of 70 nm width. We demonstrate its integration into a deployed entanglement-based QKD system that bridges the gap between laboratory prototypes and practical quantum communication hardware.

papers.title: Path Integrals on Functional Lattices
papers.abstract: Path integrals in quantum field theory are commonly approached through finite-dimensional approximations, but existence and regulator independence of the infinite-dimensional limit require separate analysis. We introduce a scheme in which spacetime remains continuous and the field is expanded in a discrete complete family of localized functions, called a functional lattice. Truncation to finite-dimensional functional subspaces yields ordinary finite-dimensional integrals while leaving the continuum differential operator unchanged. For the massive free Euclidean scalar field, we prove convergence of the finite-dimensional covariance operators and normalized generating functionals by a Galerkin argument. The limit is independent of the compatible functional lattice: any sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces dense in the quadratic-form domain converges to the same continuum covariance and generating functional. A direct Minkowski construction is obtained at fixed Feynman regulator $i\epsilon$, followed by the distributional limit $\epsilon\downarrow0$. For interacting theories, each truncation gives an ordinary non-Gaussian integral. At fixed perturbative order, convergence follows when the finite-resolution graph integrands converge pointwise and admit an integrable majorant independent of the functional resolution. Numerical results for one-dimensional $\phi^4$ theory approach the known first- and second-order mass-gap coefficients, while four-dimensional calculations exhibit the expected mass divergence and logarithmic wave-function renormalization. Thus functional lattices provide a continuum-space approach to path integrals with mathematically controlled limits in the cases considered here.

papers.title: BO-COMM: Bidirectional Optical System for Simultaneous Localization and Communication in Swarm Robotics
papers.abstract: Swarm robotics experiments require observations of robot pose and operational state, together with mechanisms for returning environmental information to the robots. Shared channel wireless communication can face contention and congestion as concurrent reporting demands increase, while a static visual marker does not itself convey changing robot states. We present BO-COMM, an optical system that combines pose estimation and dynamic state reporting with optical downstream interaction. A camera observes circular LED arrays mounted on Colias IV robots with CEU-PLUS extension units.Ring-based voting estimates robot centers, and the spatial LED pattern provides orientation and an encoded state. A projector supplies spatial environmental cues, while an infrared module provides a separate command channel. Processing-time measurements, path-following and color-reporting experiments, and a multi-pheromone demonstration illustrate the operation of this architecture in a planar arena. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining optical pose and state observations with environmental feedback in the tested hardware and arena configuration.

papers.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
papers.abstract: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/\eta$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/\eta$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/\eta$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

papers.title: An Exact Penalty Method for Large-Scale Equality-Constrained Nonlinear Optimization
papers.abstract: We present an exact penalty method for equality-constrained nonlinear optimization. Our approach transforms the smooth, constrained problem into a sequence of nonsmooth, unconstrained problems by penalizing the constraint violation by its Euclidean norm. An outer loop updates the penalty parameter and the subproblem tolerances, while an inner loop solves each penalized subproblem with a quadratic regularization method. The method also includes a local infeasibility detection mechanism, an extrapolation strategy for warm-starting subproblems, and nonmonotone acceptance rules. We establish global convergence to first-order stationary points under a bounded penalty parameter assumption, with a worst-case complexity of \(\mathcal{O}(|\log \epsilon|\,\epsilon^{-2})\) inner iterations. We implement the method in Penelopt, an open-source Julia solver for constrained nonlinear optimization. On \(224\) problems from the CUTEst collection, Penelopt is competitive with IPOPT and more robust than the recent solvers MadNLP and Uno. These results establish exact penalty methods as a practical alternative to conventional methods for solving equality-constrained nonlinear optimization problems. To the best of our knowledge, Penelopt is the first practical implementation of an exact penalty method for large-scale constrained nonlinear optimization.

papers.title: A Finite-Rate Selection Law for Annealed Gibbs Sampling
papers.abstract: Annealed Gibbs sampling samples a multimodal model by redrawing one variable at a time from its conditional distribution as the temperature falls from a high value, where the distribution is broad, to the target temperature. Each run ends in a single mode, and unbiased Monte Carlo estimates require the runs to end in each mode in proportion to its probability under the model. At a finite cooling rate this can fail. We measure the error by $c$, the fraction of the model's log-odds between two modes that the samples retain. In the Curie--Weiss model, where a weak external field favors one of two modes, each run selects its mode near the transition at which the modes form, and rarely switches once they have separated. Near the transition, the random fluctuations of the Gibbs updates still outweigh the weak field, which therefore biases the choice of mode only slightly. Building on the selection probability of Kondepudi and coworkers, we derive a law for $c$ that agrees with an exact computation to within $2\%$ on nine linear cooling ramps. For the Hopfield model, whose modes are stored patterns and their negatives, we derive a factor by which competition among patterns raises $c$. The $c$ measured over random pattern sets lies within $3$--$6\%$ of its prediction, but single pattern sets depart from it, contrary to its derivation.

papers.title: Speech Emotion Recognition Across Languages: Prosodic Patterns and Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates the prosodic patterns of emotional speech across Chinese (CN), German (DE), and English (EN), with a focus on acoustic characteristics. Using ANOVA and mixed-effects modeling, we reveal cross-linguistic and emotion-specific prosodic patterns. A comparative analysis of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) performance demonstrates that humans outperform Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) models in cross-lingual tasks, while SSL models show significant improvement in cross-lingual SER through an efficient fine-tuning process, achieving performance competitive with native human speakers. The study also analyzes the performance of Speech Emotion Diarization (SED) between models and humans, highlighting the effectiveness of SSL models in transfer learning scenarios. These findings emphasize the interplay between universal prosodic features (e.g., intensity, pitch) and language-specific factors. Moreover, the SSL model's outstanding performance indicates the potential value of these acoustic features in emotion processing, implying possible advancements in cross-lingual emotion recognition through refined training techniques.

papers.title: Do Larger Fully Connected Neural Networks Generalize Better?
papers.abstract: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better than a shallower architecture on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. We compare two architectures under two learning rates and two L2-regularization settings, producing eight configurations. The architectures contain 95,410 and 561,470 trainable parameters, respectively, an approximately 5.9-fold difference. Checkpoints and the final configuration are selected by validation loss, and all configurations are evaluated on a held-out test set. The selected larger configuration achieves 89.82% validation accuracy and 88.77% test accuracy. Selecting the lowest-validation-loss configuration within each architecture yields test accuracies of 88.77% and 88.52%, respectively, a difference of 0.25 percentage points. Across matched training settings, the larger architecture achieves higher test accuracy in only one of four comparisons. Class-level errors are concentrated among visually similar garment categories, and qualitative pixel-removal analyses suggest sensitivity to shape and boundaries. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing architectural capacity alone does not guarantee better generalization, highlighting the importance of considering optimization and regularization when selecting neural-network architectures.

papers.title: Unruh-like effects and correlation harvesting between particle detectors in uniform motion in (2+1)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime
papers.abstract: We study Gaussian-switched Unruh-DeWitt detectors coupled to a massless scalar field in the (2+1)-dimensional Minkowski vacuum and following four classes of uniformly accelerated trajectories: linear, catenary, cusped, and circular motion. We first determine how the single-detector transition probability and effective temperature depend on acceleration and the torsion-to-acceleration ratio $\bar{b}$, whose continuous variation connects these four trajectory classes. We find that both quantities generally increase with acceleration, while their dependence on $\bar{b}$ can become nonmonotonic depending on the energy gap. We also examine a correlation-harvesting protocol by two detectors following horizontally displaced copies of the same trajectory. Increasing acceleration or separation generally suppresses the harvested concurrence and quantum mutual information, but the extent of suppression at fixed acceleration depends strongly on the trajectory class. For each of the four trajectory classes, we identify regimes of genuine entanglement harvesting in which vacuum correlations alone suffice to entangle the detectors, while the communication contribution alone cannot overcome local noise.

papers.title: Distributed Interactive Conformal Prediction for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly rely on learning-enabled components and distributed algorithms for perception, estimation, and control, introducing uncertainty that makes it challenging to satisfy mission requirements. Conformal prediction quantifies uncertainty with distribution-free guarantees, but existing methods do not address the challenging combination of dependence among robots, distributed calibration, and the distribution shift induced when calibrated uncertainty bounds modify the closed-loop system. We introduce Multi-Agent Interactive Conformal Prediction (MA-ICP), a distributed framework for computing robustness margins in heterogeneous systems to satisfy mission requirements with high probability. MA-ICP aggregates robot-level nonconformity scores, which measure errors in modeled or estimated quantities, into one mission-level score per robot class, allowing dependence among robots within each mission. Mission-level scores and quantiles are computed using neighbor-to-neighbor communication in a finite number of communication rounds. Updating the robustness margins changes robot trajectories and distributed algorithm outputs, so we use class-dependent score sensitivities to upper bound the shift in mission-level scores. We then establish calibration-conditional coverage guarantees per robot class for the updated margins. We demonstrate MA-ICP on cooperative payload control, formation control with obstacle avoidance, and distributed target tracking missions.

papers.title: Grounding Collaborative Agents in Group Cognition
papers.abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.

papers.title: Optical Motion Sensing for Piezoelectric-Resonator-Based Power Converters
papers.abstract: Piezoelectric components present a promising alternative to conventional magnetics for miniaturized, high-frequency power converters. While high-Q piezoelectric resonators have demonstrated high efficiencies and large power densities in prototype high-frequency dc-dc converters, their optimal operating conditions are sensitive to temperature fluctuations and load variations. Therefore, robust closed-loop control is essential for practical deployment. Electrical approaches for sensing motional current may compromise the electrical isolation and electromagnetic interference (EMI) immunity inherently provided by the mechanical nature of these resonators. Here, we present an optical motion sensing approach for piezoelectric power converters. The optical sensing system comprises a laser, fiber optics, and a photodetector. The proposed approach uses optical interference to monitor the mechanical displacement in real time. The resulting optical signal carries both the amplitude and phase of the mechanical motion, which are necessary for closed-loop control. We experimentally characterize and validate this optical motion sensing approach using a 45-kHz piezoelectric resonator driven by a GaN half bridge with input voltages up to 45 V. We further experimentally demonstrate closed-loop control using the proposed optical motion sensing for a 99-kHz isolated piezoelectric converter. These initial results establish a viable pathway toward optically closed-loop control of piezoelectric power converters.

papers.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
papers.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

papers.title: Automorphism groups of Severi--Brauer varieties of odd prime degree over $\mathbb{Q}$
papers.abstract: We prove that the only non-trivial finite subgroup of automorphism group of non-trivial Severi--Brauer variety of odd prime degree $p$ over the field of rational numbers is $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}.$

papers.title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
papers.abstract: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

papers.title: Parallel batch scheduling for optimizing hospital sterilization operations: arc-flow formulations, column generation and Lagrangian heuristics for flowtime minimization
papers.abstract: In a recent work by Schlembach et al., the problem of optimally managing sterilization operations in hospitals has been modeled as a machine scheduling problem with parallel batch processing and minimum flowtime objective, and heuristically solved by column generation. We draw upon this approach, developing arc-flow formulations and related column-generation procedures, using an exact dynamic programming algorithm to solve the pricing problems. We further derive Lagrangian relaxations based on minimum cost flows and shortest paths, with subgradient optimization and the volume algorithm guiding batch generation. A makespan bound for schedules minimizing total flow time provides a finite horizon when no operational limit is known. Computational experiments on literature benchmarks and more challenging generated instances demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. The arc-flow model solves all literature benchmark instances to proven optimality within seconds, while the Lagrangian heuristics deliver high-quality schedules with substantially reduced computational effort.

papers.title: Who Gets to Do Computing Research? Rethinking Access, Funding, and the Cost of Research -- How do we ensure that everyone with the ideas, ability, and desire to contribute to computing research can do so?
papers.abstract: The future of computing research will be shaped not just by the questions we ask, but also by who has the opportunity to pursue them. Major investments in advanced computing, including artificial/super intelligence (AI) and quantum computing (QC), are expanding opportunities for discovery and innovation. Pursuing these opportunities requires more than a promising idea: researchers also need time, infrastructure, technical expertise, and support to compete for and administer funding. Access to these resources varies across institutions and may shape who can participate and which research directions they can pursue. A healthy computing research ecosystem depends on research taking place at institutions with different missions and resources, not only at the best-resourced ones. Computing research spans a broad spectrum of resource requirements, from theoretical work and software developed by small teams to experiments requiring specialized hardware, large datasets, and substantial technical support. Preserving opportunities across this range requires understanding not only the resources needed to conduct research, but also the costs of securing them. What does it cost an institution -- and an individual researcher -- to participate in computing research? This article invites computing researchers, university leaders, funding agencies, and industry partners to examine how funding structures, access to infrastructure, administrative responsibilities, and institutional expectations affect research opportunities, and how meaningful pathways can be preserved across institutions with different missions and resources.

papers.title: T2ISpec: Benchmarking Speculative Decoding for Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generators produce detailed images but remain slow at inference. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost, yet its behavior across the rendering requirements of T2I prompts remains insufficiently understood. We introduce T2ISpec, a benchmark of 1,400 prompts balanced across seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels. It evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators by latency, work performed by the target model, and image quality. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) aggregate results hide large differences between topics, (2) alignment and preference scores can disagree with prompt constraint satisfaction, and (3) large reductions in target work can yield limited latency gains. Motivated by these findings, we propose TopicRoute, a plugin that combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls without retraining the generator. Across six model--method pairs, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 1.0308x over the native methods, and the speedup carries over to external prompts with the same settings, while quality gains and losses vary across configurations.

papers.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
papers.abstract: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

papers.title: 3D-EMCAD: Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoding for Volumetric Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.abstract: Encoder-decoder networks are widely used for volumetric brain tumor segmentation, yet recent trends favor high-capacity decoders that incur steep computational costs in 3D at high spatial resolutions. The Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoder (EMCAD) is a lightweight decoder that achieves strong accuracy at very low cost, but it has been validated only in 2D. Here, we extend EMCAD to volumetric segmentation (3D-EMCAD) by converting all operations to 3D and replacing standard normalization layers with group normalization to suit the small batch sizes of volumetric training. To isolate the impact of decoder choice, we evaluate five decoders: the proposed 3D-EMCAD, a vanilla SegResNet decoder, an Attention U-Net decoder, UNet++, and a plain U-Net decoder using an identical 3D SegResNet encoder and training protocol on BraTS 2020 (369 cases, three-fold cross-validation). The five decoders yield statistically indistinguishable performance: their mean Dice scores span only 0.0071, less than the fold-to-fold variation of most models, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows no significant difference between 3D-EMCAD and three of the four baselines. Importantly, 3D-EMCAD achieves this shared accuracy with the fewest decoder parameters (1.15 M) and operations (8.6 G), requiring $7.3\times$ fewer operations than UNet++, which scores no higher. These findings demonstrate that decoder capacity beyond a modest budget offers no measurable benefit for volumetric brain tumor segmentation.

papers.title: RAGA: Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars from a Single Photo
papers.abstract: Avatars created from a single photo are fixed once made: regions the photo never showed, such as the back of a garment, are hallucinated and remain that way. We present Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars (RAGA), a full-body Gaussian avatar that is created from a single image in about one second and can be refreshed whenever new images of the same person become available, without retraining or gradient-based optimization. RAGA maps each new observation into canonical UV space, accumulates it as visibility- and angle-weighted running sums, and re-decodes the fused map with the same decoder used for the photo. Although this decoder is trained only on single images, it makes use of the fused evidence. On 163 clips from five datasets, RAGA created from one photo outperforms LHM, LHM++ and IDOL, including on three datasets never used in training. Refreshing from later frames adds 0.49 dB PSNR overall and 0.68 dB on views turned at least 135{\deg} from the photo, where SSIM and LPIPS also improve. Given the same 16 images on all clips, LHM++ gains 0.15 dB, against 0.48 dB for RAGA. Creating an avatar takes 1.08 s and animating it 48.1 ms per frame on a laptop RTX 3080 GPU, with body fitting and matting included in creation and pose estimation included in animation. Code will be released on GitHub.

papers.title: Multi-Sensor Fusion for False-Alarm Reduction by Timed Electromechanical Corroboration
papers.abstract: A physician checks the clinical electrocardiogram against other observations. A wearable monitor has no physician. This paper shows that a mechanical sensor worn beside the electrocardiogram can take over that check, and that the right added sensors lower false alarms further. A beat is accepted only when a mechanical contraction follows at the delay learned for the wearer. Beat-shaped artifacts injected into resting and exercise recordings passed the electrocardiogram alone almost every time. A seismocardiogram or phonocardiogram as the second channel rejected most while keeping nearly all true beats, strongly at rest and partly during exercise. Shifting the mechanical signal in time removed the benefit. A detection criterion scores an added sensor by the part of its response that the sensors in place cannot predict. With four sensors, this score ranked the sets as their measured false-alarm rates did. With the two sensors it selected, 6.2 percent of the artifacts passed while 95 percent of true beats were kept, half the rate of the best single sensor. In integer arithmetic on a low-cost microcontroller, the detector made the same decisions as the software. These rates come from injected artifacts, not alarms in patients. Natural motion and clinical events remain untested.

papers.title: The marginal sine-Gordon field theory
papers.abstract: At $\beta_*^2=8\pi$ we construct the two-dimensional sine--Gordon vacuum from a noncompact real lattice field with nearest-neighbor kinetic energy, positive cosine activity and zero Dirichlet data. Its mass $M$ is the lower edge of the energy spectrum above the vacuum. In units of the length $a_{\rm exit}$ at which the flow leaves weak coupling it obeys $0<c_-\le M a_{\rm exit}\le c_+<\infty$ on compact positive endpoint intervals, with uniform constants. A prescribed response to a smooth background in a fixed square determines the nonlinear asymptotically free bare parameters at each sufficiently fine cutoff. In the local relativistic continuum theory the vacuum is unique, physical dilation realizes every positive mass, and literal derivatives generate the reflected Hilbert space even for finite composite and contact families. Variance and exponential moments of a derivative smear rule out a Gaussian law. A connected correlation of some finite even order above two is nonzero on separated supports. The construction gives universality for the specified finite nonnegative higher harmonics, the field equation, topological current and geometric stress tensor with their Ward, trace and contact identities, and a normalized source-transfer theorem with explicit finite-scale hypotheses.

papers.title: Convergence analysis of resonant frequency approximation in periodic Helmholtz problems
papers.abstract: We investigate resonant frequencies of the Helmholtz equation in periodic structures under quasi-periodic conditions, using approximations of the associated quasi-periodic Green function, which is represented by a lattice sum. By formulating the periodic Helmholtz problem using layer potential operators whose kernel is given by the quasi-periodic Green function, resonant frequencies correspond to characteristic values of an associated operator-valued function. Based on two approximation methods for the quasi-periodic Green function, the Ewald method and the shifted Green function method, we propose the corresponding approximation schemes for resonant frequencies. Furthermore, we establish convergence rates for the resulting approximations using Gohberg--Sigal theory, where the Ewald method yields exponential convergence, while the shifted Green function method yields algebraic convergence. Numerical computations are presented to validate and compare the proposed approximation schemes.

papers.title: Suppressing Chaos Without Silencing Excitable Oscillators
papers.abstract: A negative Lyapunov exponent is not a sufficient goal for controlling an excitable oscillator. A gain can remove chaos by removing the excitation that the model is meant to keep. This manuscript studies that failure mode in three models: the forced FitzHugh--Nagumo neuron, the forced Aliev--Panfilov cardiac cell, and the autonomous Hindmarsh--Rose neuron. Chaos is measured by the largest state Lyapunov exponent. Excitation is measured by threshold crossings, by the excursion of the fast variable, and by the firing rate. Recovery damping, tracking of an unstable periodic orbit, Pyragas delayed feedback, and a change of the fast time scale are compared on the same chaotic regimes. In the forced models, large damping and large rate changes reach regularity by silencing the cell, while tracking and delayed feedback keep firing. In the autonomous model, recovery damping raises the firing rate several-fold instead. A classical matrix-measure bound links these outcomes to the channel through which the gain acts. A constant-metric contraction certificate coexists with substantial firing only under tracking, which subtracts a gain from the fast direction.

papers.title: Sliced Tensor Operators for Large-Scale Topology Optimization
papers.abstract: Large-scale three-dimensional topology optimization is constrained by both the cost of repeatedly solving the governing finite-element equations and the memory required by these computations. Memory consumption can be controlled through specialized low-level implementations, but developing, optimizing, and extending such code requires substantial effort and hardware-specific expertise. High-level tensor programming frameworks, which support automatic differentiation, offer an attractive alternative: numerical operations can be expressed compactly, while their compilers generate highly optimized code for CPUs and GPUs. However, a direct tensor formulation creates intermediate arrays that can quickly exhaust the available memory. We address this limitation through memory-bounded tensor operators for matrix-free finite-element analysis and Galerkin multigrid. The fine-grid stiffness action is evaluated in overlapping spatial slices, and on coarse grids, the Galerkin operator is retained in a factorized representation consisting of fine-grid stiffness interpolation coefficients and precomputed local operators. This representation permits its action to be evaluated without materializing a spatially varying stiffness operator on every coarse grid, while preserving the exact Galerkin hierarchy. We implement these formulations in topax, a modular JAX library for two- and three-dimensional density-based topology optimization supporting CPUs and GPUs. On a single NVIDIA GH200, topax performs 50 design iterations for a problem with more than 809 million displacement degrees of freedom in approximately $24.5$ minutes. Across the common GPU benchmark, it is up to $13.6$ times faster than the fastest competing implementation and uses less than half the device memory for the largest problem.

papers.title: Wet-part doubling for log-concave probability measures
papers.abstract: Let $\mu$ be a log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\geqslant 2$. We study the growth of $w_\mu(t)=\mu(\{x:q_{\mu}(x)\leqslant t\})$, where $q_{\mu}$ is the Tukey half-space depth function of $\mu$. We prove that $w_{\mu}$ satisfies the doubling bound $$w_\mu(\lambda t)\leqslant C^n\lambda\left(1+\frac{\log\lambda}{n-1}\right)^{n-1}w_\mu(t)$$ for every $\lambda>1$ and $0 0$ is an absolute constant. It follows that for every $\varepsilon>0$ we may write $w_\mu(\lambda t) \leqslant A_\varepsilon^n \lambda^{1+\varepsilon}w_\mu(t)$ for some constant $A_\varepsilon>0$. We construct a family of symmetric log-concave measures in every dimension $n\geqslant2$ showing that no linear doubling bound with a dimension-dependent constant holds uniformly over this class. The proof of the doubling bound uses a pointwise comparison of half-space depth with the Cram\'{e}r transform, dual radial coordinates, and a relative entropy estimate for transverse covariance determinants.

papers.title: A Frequency-Learning Interpolation-Based Coordinate Descent Method to Optimize Parameterized Quantum Circuits on Quantum Hardware
papers.abstract: Structure-aware optimizers have been the focus of recent study for the optimization of parameters in variational quantum circuits. Many of these optimizers follow a coordinate-based paradigm, making single parameter updates by using classical approximations to the cost function generated from quantum sampling. However, the performance of structure-aware optimizers on real quantum hardware at large system size has yet to be demonstrated. Recently, Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (ICD) has been proposed to unify many of these optimizers into one framework. ICD requires a preset frequency set for interpolation, which can be theoretically derived, but for which the cost function is generally sparse over and may require manual tuning. To address these issues, we propose Frequency-learning Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (FLICD) to adaptively learn frequencies online, allowing easier scaling up to larger systems. We demonstrate that our algorithm is more accurate than an existing zeroth-order method COBYLA and requires fewer quantum resources than ICD on simulator. Using IBM quantum hardware, we execute FLICD on systems up to 100 qubits and observe robust performance with an increasing number of layers.
authors: Adam Leicester (Department of Materials Science and Engineering
Zixu Wang (Department of Materials Science and Engineering
Jian Shi (Department of Materials Science and Engineering

papers.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
papers.abstract: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

papers.title: The Dunford-Pettis property and complemented Hilbert subspaces of Sobolev martingale spaces
papers.abstract: Let $L^1_W$ be the space of integrable terminal values of martingales on a homogeneous tree whose local differences belong to a fixed matrix space $W$. We show that $L^1_W$ has the Dunford-Pettis property if and only if $W$ is spanned by its rank-one matrices. Every complemented reflexive subspace of $L^1_W$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Under the second structural condition of Ayoush, Stolyarov and Wojciechowski, the martingale fractional integral of order $\frac12$ is completely continuous and fails to be absolutely $2$-summing. This gives nonisomorphism with $L^1$ for $W\ne0$. On the $4$-ary tree we exhibit all three possible combinations of the Dunford-Pettis property and the existence of a complemented copy of $\ell^2$. In one example a bounded operator into $\ell^4$ fails to be completely continuous, although every bounded operator into a Hilbert space is completely continuous. We also prove that, for every $n\ge1$, each complemented reflexive subspace of $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{T}^n)$ is isomorphic to a Hilbert space.

papers.title: SenFabric: 3D Printing On-fabric Sensing Mechanisms for Smart Textiles
papers.abstract: We present SenFabric, a one-step fabrication technique that 3D prints conductive TPU directly onto existing fabric. Rather than compensating for conductive material instability, SenFabric uses geometry-driven resistive structures in which motion changes conductive contact and reconfigures the effective path, producing characteristic signal responses that remain distinguishable despite variation in absolute resistance. We introduce four sensing primitives, slide, press, stretch, and bend, with geometric variables that control activation force, deformation range, and resolution, and a browser-based tool that adapts them to user-supplied outlines and generates routing, pins, and printable models. Four applications demonstrate wearable sensing, human-robot interaction, garment interfaces, and animal wearables, while evaluations show geometry-dominated sensing, cross-motion selectivity, and stable response under repeated use.

papers.title: Efficient phase-only wavefront shaping at 250 kHz for multimode fiber endomicroscopy
papers.abstract: Wavefront shaping through multimode fibers (MMFs) enables diffraction-limited fluorescence imaging with hair-thin probes, at a speed and light budget bounded by the wavefront modulator. Existing modulators provide at most two of three key characteristics: high refresh rate, (high) modal dimensionality, and light efficiency. Here, we demonstrate wavefront control through an MMF using a tailored phase-only microelectromechanical modulator that combines all three, with 8,192 elements arranged in a 32 x 256 array, 7-bit phase control, and a 250 kHz full-frame refresh rate. Direct on-axis phase modulation delivers 70+/-5% of the incident light into the modulated field and eliminates both off-axis encoding optical losses and hologram computation. The generated foci at the distal end of the fiber remain isotropic with high fidelity. We use singular-value decomposition analysis of the measured transmission to identify the effective degrees of freedom of our system. By scanning the focus at multiple depths, we demonstrate volumetric fluorescence imaging. These results open a new operating regime for adaptive in vivo multimode-fiber endoscopy.

papers.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

papers.title: Economic cap coverings for log-concave measures
papers.abstract: Let $\mu$ be a log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Write $q_\mu$ for its half-space depth, $W_t=\{q_\mu \leqslant t\}$ for its wet part, and $w_\mu(t)=\mu(W_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, we construct a cover of $W_t$ by half-spaces of measure at most $A_nt$, with cardinality bounded by $$D_n\frac{w_\mu(t)-w_\mu(a_nt)}{t},$$ where the constants depend only on $n$. For each $0<\varepsilon\leqslant 1$ we also construct a cover by half-spaces of measure at most $(1+\varepsilon)t$, with cardinality bounded by $$B_n\varepsilon^{-(n-1)/2}\frac{w_\mu(t)-w_\mu(a_nt)}{t}.$$ The exponent $(n-1)/2$ is optimal for $n\geqslant 2$, as shown by the Gaussian example.
