papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

papers.title: Interface-aware dynamic mode decomposition with control for partitioned multiphysics systems
papers.abstract: We develop an interface-aware dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) formulation for multiphysics systems, within an optimization-based partitioned coupling framework. The finite-element interface-input operator is projected onto the reduced space and kept fixed during identification, while the unknown state-dependent local dynamics are learned from trajectory data. The common interface control is recomputed online by minimizing the mismatch between the reconstructed physical interface quantities. The formulation accommodates local subproblems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and differential--algebraic equations (DAEs). For a DAE subproblem, tangent projection identifies the state dynamics, whereas a residualized normal regression identifies the pressure balance and provides an algebraic pressure reconstruction. We further propose regularized quadratic correction DMDc to enrich the tangent dynamics and, for DAEs, the normal pressure balance through jointly fitted linear and compact quadratic operators. Feature normalization and block-dependent regularization control the enlarged regression while retaining the prescribed interface operators and identified DAE geometry. The proposed framework is evaluated on problems involving both ODE--ODE and DAE--ODE couplings. The numerical results demonstrate accurate predictions and stable long-time behavior.

papers.title: When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.

papers.title: RecallWorld: Episodic Memory for Persistent Embodied Video World Models
papers.abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.

papers.title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
papers.abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

papers.title: Note on polychromatic coloring of hereditary hypergraph families III
papers.abstract: For every integer $h\ge4$ we construct a hereditary family of hypergraphs with $m_2=h$ and \[ m_3\ge 2(h-1)+2\left\lfloor\frac{h-1}{3}\right\rfloor+1 \approx \frac{8}{3}m_2. \] This improves the lower bound $m_3\ge 2m_2$ from the preceding notes for every $m_2\ge4$. We also show that the worst-case integrality gap of the weighted transversal problem over hereditary families with $m_2\le h$ is between $h-1$ and $5000h$. As a consequence, every such family admits strong $\varepsilon$-nets of size at most $5000h/\varepsilon$.

papers.title: Quantitative Convergence of the Spherical Brownian Motion collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau Equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish the quantitative convergence of the spherical Brownian motion (SBM) collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau equation via Wasserstein distances. When used as numerical method, it enjoys linear complexity $O(N)$ in particle number $N$, and conserves the momentum and energy almost surely. Moreover, only random grouping and sampling are needed for simulations without further numerical discretization. In the first part, we identify the large particle mean field limit of the system, and the Wasserstein convergence to the limit is justified through a coupling similar to the recent work for the Nanbu type Monte Carlo method \cite{BorghiPareschi2025}. The key difference is that the particles in our coupled shadow system are not i.i.d. due to the perfect matching. In the second part, the convergence of the mean field dynamics to the Landau solution is justified by the relative entropy with a bound $O(\tau^2)$, being $\tau$ the stepsize. This results in an $O(\tau)$ bound for the Wasserstein distance error. A crucial technical tool in the convergence in relative entropy is to provide suitable bounds on the derivatives of the logarithmic density or score function in the mean field dynamics. The combination of these estimates leads to the full convergence of the squared Wasserstein distance with order $O(N^{-1/2}+\tau^2)$ for the numerical scheme in $d=3$.

papers.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
papers.abstract: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

papers.title: A $C_2$-cofinite non-rational principal $W$-algebra of type $D_4$
papers.abstract: We show that a simple principal $W$-algebra can be $C_2$-cofinite and non-rational. For $\mathcal W=\mathcal W_{-38/7}(D_4,f_{\mathrm{reg}})$ of central charge $-50$, D. Xie predicted seventeen irreducible modules and a logarithmic module of lowest conformal weight $-2$. We determine the Zhu algebra $A(\mathcal W)$ and the Poisson algebra $R_{\mathcal W}=\mathcal W/C_2(\mathcal W)$. Both have dimension $18$, and $A(\mathcal W)\cong\mathbb{C}^{16}\times\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. We construct all seventeen irreducible $\mathcal W$-modules using the realization of $\mathcal W$ as a diagonal coset in $L_{-14/3}(D_4)\otimes L_1(D_4)$ and our previous classification of irreducible $L_{-14/3}(D_4)$-modules in the category $\mathcal O$. We also construct an indecomposable $L_{-14/3}(D_4)$-module and use the coset realization to obtain an indecomposable logarithmic $\mathcal W$-module. Its lowest generalized $L(0)$-eigenspace is two-dimensional, and $L(0)$ acts on this space by a nontrivial Jordan block with eigenvalue $-2$.

papers.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Cayley Regression for Finite Groups with a Cyclic Subgroup of Index Two
papers.abstract: A finite group $G$ is a Cayley regression if every generalized Cayley graph of $G$ is isomorphic to a Cayley graph of $G$, and a $k$-Cayley regression if this holds for all such graphs of valency at most $k$. We show that the dihedral group $D_{2n}$, $n\geq2$, is a $2$-Cayley regression if and only if it is a $3$-Cayley regression, which holds exactly when $n$ is a prime power, and that for $k\geq4$ it is a $k$-Cayley regression if and only if $n$ is an odd prime power or $n\in\{2,4\}$. Groups with a cyclic subgroup of index two that are neither cyclic nor dihedral are not even $2$-Cayley regressions; consequently, a group with a cyclic subgroup of index two is a Cayley regression if and only if it is isomorphic to $C_2$, $C_4$, $C_6$, $C_{10}$, or $D_{2n}$ with $n$ as above. Finally, every split metacyclic group $C_m\rtimes C_q$ with $m>2$ and odd $q\geq3$ is not a $2$-Cayley regression.

papers.title: Conceptual Design of a 5 MV High-Voltage System for a Compact Orbitron Fusion Device
papers.abstract: The high-voltage system is a key part of the puzzle toward achieving net-positive fusion power in a compact Orbitron device. This paper presents a conceptual engineering design for a 5 MV, 20 mA, 100 kW HV system for a next-generation Orbitron, serving as an upper-bound design point for the HV system. The MC-TRANS++ 0-D code is used to set the load requirements: a 1 m long, 0.45 m first-wall-radius central cell, 2.5 T on-axis and 10 T mirror-throat fields, and a 5 MV radial potential drop sustaining supersonic rotation ($M = 4.8$). This delivers a triple product of $5.8 \times 10^{21}$ keV s /m3 and $Q_{sci}$ = 8.5. The HV power supply integrates an AC-DC converter, a SiC full-bridge inverter, a CLLC resonant network with an air-core step-up transformer, and feeds a 120-stage parallel-fed series-cascaded rectifier operating at 250 kHz. At full load, this architecture yields an end-to-end efficiency of 85%, much higher than the 60% typical of triode-driven MV-class power supplies. The 5 MV voltage is delivered to a radially nested 50-gap bushing system that interfaces pressurized insulating gas to high vacuum, using brazed alumina spacers with a corrugated profile. The design draws directly on the measured behavior of a previously demonstrated 300 kV prototype, from which six quantitative lessons are extracted and mapped onto the 5 MV design. Electrostatic simulations of the complete assembly at rated voltage show maximum surface fields of 30.3 MV/m on the corona rings, 7.7 MV/m at the cathode triple junction, and average vacuum-gap fields ranging from 5.5 to 40 MV/m. These field strengths remain below breakdown thresholds due to the implementation of triple-junction shielding, insulation corrugation, and axial magnetic insulation at 2.5-10 T. The conceptual system has a form factor of 2.7 meters in diameter and 6.5 meters in length, projected to deliver a net power output of 86-171 kWe.

papers.title: Global existence and decay estimates for classical solutions to 2D compressible micropolar fluid equations with vacuum
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider the Cauchy problem for the two-dimensional compressible micropolar fluid equations with far field vacuum. Under the assumption that the initial energy is sufficiently small, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of strong and classical solutions, allowing for large oscillations in the initial data. The key to the proof is to derive {\it a priori} decay estimates for the pressure, the velocity gradient, and the microrotational velocity, which enable us to close the bootstrap argument. We also handle the difficulties arising from the coupling between the velocity field and the microrotational velocity.

papers.title: Dual-Stream Event-to-Video Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.

papers.title: UACR: Uncertainty-Aware Collaborative Routing for Explainable Industrial Anomaly Inspection
papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires not only accurate anomaly discrimination but also trustworthy explanations for operators, while satisfying the strict latency constraints of online inspection. Existing methods, however, typically apply a fixed computational path to all samples, making it difficult to strike a good balance among detection accuracy, inference efficiency, and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose UACR, an uncertainty-aware collaborative routing framework for explainable industrial anomaly inspection. UACR aims to deliver reliable anomaly decisions together with operator-facing explanations under the online inspection budget, while adaptively allocating computation so that ambiguous cases receive deeper scrutiny. The framework consists of two stages. Stage I, Offline Training and Routing Hyperparameter Search, learns the anomaly inspection modules and calibrates the uncertainty estimator that drives routing. Stage II, Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Routing, collaboratively dispatches each input across inspection paths according to its estimated uncertainty. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show that UACR achieves over 5.16% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline method, while reducing latency by over 31.5%. It also enhances the interpretability of industrial detection by over 15%.

papers.title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
papers.abstract: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

papers.title: InstantCoFFEA: Fast and accurate Tor flow correlation at realistic scale
papers.abstract: Tor end-to-end correlation attacks can link a client to its destination by matching traffic observed at both ends of a Tor circuit. However, their practical threat remains unclear for two reasons: existing correlation methods rely on O(N^2) pairwise processing, and prior works do not reflect the flow counts and base rates seen by realistic adversaries. We present InstantCoFFEA, which replaces exhaustive pairwise search with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval using CAGRA and introduces ranked voting. At N = 200k, InstantCoFFEA is 14.56x faster than DeepCoFFEA and improves PR-AUC from 0.94 to 0.96. We also use TorPS to estimate the flow counts and matching-pair base rates observed by relay-level and network-level adversaries. Our simulations show that realistic attacks involve substantially more candidate flows and much lower base rates than those used in prior evaluations. Under a low-base-rate setting, PR-AUC drops for all methods, but InstantCoFFEA achieves 0.53 compared with 0.42 for DeepCoFFEA. These results show that evaluating correlation attacks requires considering both computational scale and the sparsity of true matching pairs.

papers.title: Inverse problems for ZS operators and their isomorphisms, II
papers.abstract: We study isomorphic inverse spectral problems for Zakharov--Shabat operators on the unit interval with generic boundary conditions. A unitary gauge transformation reduces these problems to the corresponding problems with basic boundary conditions, with an explicit shift of the spectral parameter. Using previous results for canonical boundary conditions and four-spectra data mapping we describe isomorphic inverse spectral problems for Zakharov--Shabat operators. Moreover, study other inverse problems including replacing mappings and canonical relations.

papers.title: Anti OS Fingerprinting, Revisited: A Loadable Kernel Module for FreeBSD and What Twenty-Five Years Changed
papers.abstract: In 2001 we published a paper on an Anti OS Detection (AoD) system: a modified FreeBSD 4.3 kernel that makes a host answer the probes of an OS fingerprinting tool as if it ran another operating system. This report revisits that work on FreeBSD 15.1. We do not claim a new method. We report three things. First, the same goal is now reachable from a loadable module of about 800 lines that uses the packet filter hook interface and sets one kernel variable, without changing the kernel source. Second, the module covers both active and passive fingerprinting: Nmap 7.98 reports an exact match for Linux and for Windows 10/11, and p0f 3 reports the same systems from the connections the host opens. Third, an exact match in Nmap was not enough: a passive tool, plain FIN scans and a comparison with real hosts each exposed a mismatch that the previous step could not see. A real Windows 11 host and the final Windows personality get the same verdict from Nmap and the same signatures from p0f and JA4T; a real Linux 7.0 host is not an exact match in Nmap at all, while the personality built from Nmap's database is. We describe those mismatches, how we removed them, what the module costs, and what it still cannot hide.

papers.title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

papers.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

papers.title: Beyond Full-Context Accuracy: Context-Marginalized Evaluation of Test-Time Structure-Aware Inference in EEG-to-Image Retrieval
papers.abstract: Test-time structure-aware inference can improve cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval by exploiting relations among unlabeled test queries, but it also makes predictions depend on query-set composition. Existing evaluations typically report accuracy under a single full-query context, leaving unclear whether gains and comparative conclusions hold as context changes. We introduce Context-Marginalized Retrieval Evaluation (CMRE), which repeatedly evaluates each target query in sampled contexts using the corresponding rows of a fixed query-gallery similarity matrix. CMRE distinguishes structural exploitability, quantified by gains over independent retrieval, from context robustness, measured by same-query Top-1 context consistency. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2 across six frozen representations and six structure-aware inference rules, structure-aware inference improves full-context Top-1 accuracy by up to 20.40 percentage points over independent retrieval. However, the rule selected under full-context evaluation is no longer optimal in 17 of 24 representation-context-size conditions (70.8%). Selecting the full-context winner incurs an average loss of 2.70 percentage points and a maximum loss of 8.29 percentage points under reduced contexts. Representation rankings are likewise inference- and context-dependent: the ordering under independent retrieval is not consistently preserved under structure-aware inference. Moreover, larger retrieval gains do not necessarily imply greater context robustness, showing that retrieval effectiveness and prediction stability provide complementary views of structure-aware inference. Full-context accuracy captures one operating point of context-dependent inference. CMRE complements it by characterizing how structural gains, context consistency, and comparisons of rules and representations change with query context.

papers.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
papers.abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.

papers.title: OrthoLatentCAD: Orthographic Spatial Latents for Hand-Drawn CAD Program Generation
papers.abstract: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.

papers.title: PROSPER: LLMs as Sparse Retrievers for First-Stage Product Search
papers.abstract: Product search is a crucial component of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where first-stage retrieval should achieve high recall while ensuring efficient online deployment. Sparse retrieval remains attractive for this setting due to its interpretability and deployability, yet it suffers from severe vocabulary mismatch challenges, especially for short queries and product titles. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic capabilities, but directly applying them to sparse retrieval in product search introduces new challenges: (i) semantic expansion may distort critical literal signals such as brand names and model identifiers; and (ii) learning meaningful sparse representations is difficult in the high-dimensional vocabulary space induced by LLMs.To address these challenges, we propose PROSPER, a framework that uses LLMs as sparse retrievers for product search while explicitly preserving lexical fidelity. PROSPER combines (i) a literal residual network that alleviates lexical expansion hallucination by reinforcing underweighted literal terms through a residual compensation mechanism; and (ii) a lexical focusing window that uses top-k selection for rapid early sparsification and effective training initialization. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate that PROSPER consistently improves over existing sparse retrievers, and provides revenue gains for industrial hybrid retrieval systems.

papers.title: NP-Completeness of the Three-Dimensional Polyhedral Separation Problem
papers.abstract: Bone tumor resection planning motivates the following geometric problem. Given tumor points and healthy-bone points in three-dimensional space, find cutting planes that separate the tumor from the surrounding bone. To avoid tumor seeding, the cutting planes must not pass through the tumor. Given a positive integer k, select at most k closed halfspaces whose intersection contains all tumor points, while minimizing the total weight of healthy-bone points strictly inside this intersection. We formalize this problem and prove that its threshold decision version is NP-complete. Consequently, the corresponding optimization problem is NP-hard.

papers.title: Numerical approximation of the Hilfer fractional derivative using orthogonal Quasi-Polynomials
papers.abstract: A numerical approach based on a composite Gaussian quadrature for the Hilfer fractional derivative is presented. This approach employs quasi-polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to the weight function on the interval $(0,1)$. As special cases, the Riemann--Liouville and Caputo fractional derivatives are obtained. Error bounds for the approximation are derived. To confirm the convergence rates as well as the high efficiency of the new approach, numerical examples are provided.

papers.title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
papers.abstract: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

papers.title: CrossPanel: Exposing the Answer-Evidence Gap in Scientific Figure Understanding
papers.abstract: A correct answer to a scientific-figure question can conceal an incorrect account of the experiment. Reading evidence across panels requires keeping each observation attached to the object and conditions that give it meaning. We introduce CrossPanel, a benchmark of 2,650 human-reviewed questions that exposes this answer-evidence gap. Its tasks combine parallel observations or follow dependent queries, while a response audit separates object selection, experimental conditions, cross-panel binding, and local readout. Across 15 vision-language models on 251 diagnostic questions, 8.42%-56.64% of correct answers contain explicit factual errors. The audit distinguishes coherent readings of the wrong target from incorrect readings of the right one. Controlled interventions then test how these failures can be repaired: verified object-condition hints, which withhold the requested measurement, raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's target-query success by 22.81 percentage points on 57 questions, while additional image tiles alone yield little improvement. Other models benefit most from combining both forms of assistance. These findings identify experimental attribution as a distinct requirement alongside local perception, and make both measurable beyond final-answer accuracy.
authors: Zhengyang Lu (University of Science and Technology of China)
Ziyang Ling (University of Science and Technology of China)
Huan Li (University of Science and Technology of China)
Yibo Qiu (University of Science and Technology of China)

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoors in Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

papers.title: Finite-difference neural policy iteration for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi equations
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-difference neural policy iteration method for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations. Artificial viscosity yields a monotone finite-difference operator, and neural networks approximate the linear equations of semi-discrete policy iteration using local stencil values. This avoids global tensor-grid storage. For measurable feedbacks, we bound the propagation of evaluation, terminal, gradient, and control optimization errors by a geometrically weighted sum. Discrete comparison, consistency, and vanishing viscosity relate the approximation to the original degenerate equation. On coupled manufactured problems with rank-deficient diffusion, the method achieves lower mean errors than direct physics-informed neural networks at every tested dimension from five to fifty under equal training time. At fifty dimensions and $900$ seconds, the mean relative $L^2$ error over three paired seeds is about $40\%$ lower. Two-dimensional refinement attains $0.297\%$ error against the original degenerate solution, with independent grid references separating approximation error from viscosity bias. In a twenty-dimensional game with finite control sets, reusing policies reduces the measured time to a relative error of $5\%$ by $24.3\%$ compared with direct minimization of the same discrete residual with fresh samples at every update.

papers.title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.

papers.title: A two-sided continued-fraction criterion for the Erd\H{o}s-Moser equation and Erd\H{o}s's 1949 problem
papers.abstract: We give a two-sided continued-fraction criterion for the Erd\H{o}s--Moser equation $1^k+2^k+\dots+(m-1)^k=m^k$. Writing $m=k/\log 2+3/2+\gamma_m/m$, Gallot, Moree and Zudilin showed that a solution yields a convergent of $\log 2/(2N)$, for a known divisor $N$ of $k$, followed by a large partial quotient. We show that an explicit two-sided estimate for $\gamma_m$, from our earlier centre-of-mass work, restricts this partial quotient, for each value of $\gcd(k/N,2m-3)$, to two consecutive values, or to three in the exceptional case that an integer lies in an explicit interval of relative length $O(1/m)$. This excludes the first index left open by their computation and, without extending their continued-fraction computation, raises the lower bound for a nontrivial solution from $m>2.71\cdot 10^{1667658416}$ to $m>6.26\cdot 10^{1667658425}$. The same criterion gives an effective form of the asymptotic results of Best and te Riele on Erd\H{o}s's 1949 problem on the largest term of $1^n+\dots+(m-1)^n$. We determine all 50 pairs $(m,n)$ with $m m^n$; in particular, the smallest example found by Best and te Riele in 1976 is the smallest such pair, a question they had left open. For $n<0.69\cdot 10^{399}$ we also determine the 51 elements of O'Bryant's exceptional set $A_2$ and all 101 terms of OEIS A129935 below this bound, one of them not previously listed, and settle several conjectures recorded in the OEIS. Finally, using only the upper bound in our estimate for $\gamma_m$ and its positivity, we show that the second part of Erd\H{o}s's problem, the existence of infinitely many such pairs, is equivalent to the infinitude of $A_2$ and to the existence of infinitely many even-index convergents $p_j/q_j$ of $\log 2$ with $p_j$ even, $q_j$ odd and $q_j(q_j\log 2-p_j)<\Theta(q_j)$, where $\Theta(q)=(\log 2)/3+O(q^{-2})$ is explicit.

papers.title: SemGuard: Semantics-Decoupled Watermarking for Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Gaussian Splatting provides an efficient representation for high-fidelity rendering of static and dynamic 3D scenes, motivating the copyright protection of Gaussian assets. In CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, a universal message decoder pretrained on textual watermark representations is subsequently applied to visual features containing both watermark information and scene-dependent semantics. However, text-only pretraining does not explicitly account for the semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. To address this challenge, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that learns to suppress scene-dependent semantic interference during universal message decoder pretraining. Specifically, SemGuard combines message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked scene images, constructing training representations with controllable semantic interference relevant to the target Gaussian assets. A progressive semantic interference curriculum gradually increases the contribution of visual features, allowing the decoder to first learn reliable message representations and then adapt to increasingly strong scene-dependent semantic interference. After pretraining for a given message length and semantic image pool, the decoder is frozen and reused across multiple Gaussian assets whose visual semantics are covered by the pretraining data. Experiments on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets demonstrate improved rendering fidelity alongside reliable watermark extraction, while evaluations on static assets further show enhanced robustness against image-space distortions.

papers.title: LoopSeek: Decoupling System One Search from System Two Answering for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.

papers.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
papers.abstract: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.

papers.title: The shortest figure-eight geodesics on random hyperbolic surfaces
papers.abstract: We consider primitive unoriented figure-eight geodesics on a closed hyperbolic surface of genus $g$ sampled from Weil--Petersson measure. The shortest of these geodesics realizes the non-simple systole. He, Shen, Wu and Xue proved that its length is tight after centering at $a_g=\log g-\log\log g$. We prove that, as $g\to\infty$, the point process of centered lengths converges to a Poisson process on $\mathbb R$ with intensity $e^s\,ds/(8\pi^2)$. Its first arrival gives a reflected Gumbel limit for the centered systole $M_g$. We also prove convergence of the marked process in which each figure-eight carries the three cuff lengths of its supporting pair of pants, normalized by their sum. In the limiting process, the third cuff accounts for half the perimeter. The two winding cuffs, ordered at random, divide the other half uniformly. These splits are independent across points and independent of the limiting lengths. Uniform exponential bounds on both tails of $M_g$ give convergence of all fixed polynomial moments. At the critical exponent $-1$, we obtain $\mathbb E_g e^{-M_g}\sim(\log g)/(16\pi^2)$.

papers.title: Self-prediction residuals improve single-pass detection of wrong-object boxes in grounded vision-language models
papers.abstract: Grounded vision-language models write boxes as text, and the mean probability of their coordinate tokens says little about whether a box is right. We study a single-pass signal for boxes on another object, which matter when only the object counts. A linear map, fitted per model to its own answers without labels, reads a box from the hidden state before writing. Its disagreement with the written box, the self-prediction residual, flags boxes on another object although the read-out is far less accurate; the residual's weight was fixed with labels on two models. On a replication list of 1,200 RefCOCOg test items, the residual, averaged over six models, raises the detection of these errors for each of fifteen single-pass scores, by 0.026 to 0.049 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on a label-free probe and probes trained on 2,000 labelled items. Over all errors, adding it to the label-free probe moves AUROC, averaged over the models, by less than 0.02 (95% interval). With a fifth of answers reviewed, the share of all errors caught moves from 0.518 to 0.524, that of boxes on another object from 0.505 to 0.607 (post hoc): the residual changes which errors are found, not how many, and in cost-weighted recall it breaks even when such a box costs about 0.86 times another error, and its gain is positive in point estimate at equal costs. These gains come from RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images.

papers.title: Strictness of the containment of Kirk's asymptotic contractions in a class defined by two quasi-metrics
papers.abstract: Kirk's asymptotic contractions are defined by moduli $\psi_n$ which converge uniformly on $[0,\infty)$ to a Boyd--Wong function and are evaluated at the distance $d(x,y)$ only. A relaxed class, in which the estimate involves a lower and an upper quasi-metric built from the four distances $d(x,y)$, $d(x,Ty)$, $d(Tx,y)$ and $d(Tx,Ty)$, was recently shown to contain Kirk's class and to admit the same fixed point conclusion. It was left open whether the containment is strict. We prove that it is. The separating maps form a family of radial damping maps $T(x)=\lambda(\norm{x})x$ on a normed space, where $\lambda\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\rho]$ is continuous, $0\le\rho<1$, nonconstant and periodic: every such map is a relaxed asymptotic contraction with explicit linear moduli, whereas its one-step dispersion at a fixed distance is unbounded, so that no finite Kirk modulus exists. A slowly modulated nonperiodic damping law is treated as well. We further show that strictness can occur only when the image $T(X)$ is not relatively compact: in a complete space, if $T(X)$ is relatively compact, the two classes coincide, hence on a compact (in particular finite) space no separating example exists. Applications to semi-active vibration isolation with amplitude-dependent damping and to digital maturity gaps in the digital transformation of small and medium-sized enterprises are discussed, and numerical illustrations are provided.

papers.title: Strong First-Order Phase Transition in a Pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone Boson Model
papers.abstract: We propose a novel, calculable model for realizing strong first-order phase transitions in the early Universe, in which the phase transition occurs along a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB) direction. The model involves two scalar fields whose interactions exhibit collective symmetry breaking, protecting the pNGB potential from quadratically divergent radiative corrections induced by these interactions. This structure allows strong first-order phase transitions to be realized without severe parameter tuning while maintaining perturbative control. We investigate the finite-temperature effective potential and bubble nucleation dynamics, identifying parameter regions where strong first-order phase transitions can successfully complete. The strength and characteristic time scale of the transitions are evaluated, and the resulting gravitational-wave (GW) spectra are computed. The predicted GW signals can fall within the sensitivity ranges of planned GW experiments.

papers.title: Seeing 3D Occupancy Through Scene-Adaptive Projection
papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction infers voxel-wise geometry and semantics from multi-view images, where 2D-to-3D view transformation is a crucial step. Many existing methods adopt a backward-projection paradigm, projecting uniformly distributed 3D reference points onto image planes to aggregate multi-view features. However, their scene-agnostic sampling patterns overlook the non-uniform distribution of scene geometry, allocating many references to empty space and reducing sampling efficiency under a fixed sampling budget. To address this challenge, we propose SAP, a scene-adaptive projection framework that leverages depth-based geometric priors to guide view transformation. Specifically, we back-project metric depth maps predicted by a frozen depth model into 3D space to obtain geometric priors. To leverage these priors, we design a Scene-Adaptive Projection Encoder comprising two complementary components. First, Prior-Guided Reference Generation constructs a hybrid reference set for feature sampling, allocating references within prior-supported height regions and retaining full-range sampling where valid support is unavailable. Furthermore, to account for potential spatial misalignment caused by depth estimation errors, Radial-Structured Feature Aggregation explores multiple candidate locations through learned radial offsets to aggregate potentially displaced feature evidence. Extensive experiments on Occ3D demonstrate that SAP achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves results across diverse occupancy frameworks.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

papers.title: A High-Frequency Flux-Driven DC-SQUID Threshold Detector at the Single-Microwave-Photon Energy Scale: A Numerical Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: In our recent work (Phys. Rev. B \textbf{113}, 224503 (2026)), we showed numerically that rapidly sweeping the bias current of a current-biased Josephson junction threshold detector (CBJJ-JTD) drives it out of equilibrium. This substantially reduces the effect of thermal noise on microwave detection and may enable threshold detection near the energy of a single microwave photon. The scheme requires very low damping ($\beta \leq 10^{-4}$) and a very fast bias-current sweep ($v/\beta \geq 1$), both of which are difficult to achieve with available junctions and low-pass-filtered cryogenic measurement lines. Here we propose a more experimentally accessible nonequilibrium threshold detector based on a high-frequency flux-driven direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC-SQUID) and investigate it by numerically solving the resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) equations. The applied flux drives a circulating supercurrent and sustains nonequilibrium phase dynamics throughout the bias-current sweep, removing the need for a fast sweep or for transient oscillations set by the initial phase. Using typical experimental device parameters, we calculate switching-current distributions (SCDs) with and without a microwave input for both driven and undriven SQUIDs. We quantify detection performance using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and their area under the curve (AUC). The simulations show that high-frequency flux drive reduces the impact of thermal noise and enables statistical discrimination of weak microwave pulses at the single-photon energy scale. We also numerically estimate detector characteristics such as phase selectivity and dynamic range.

papers.title: Probing tensor-polarized gluon TMDs through \texorpdfstring{$J/\psi$}{J/psi} electroproduction off the deuteron
papers.abstract: We investigate tensor-polarized gluon transverse-momentum-dependent distributions (TMDs) in semi-inclusive $J/\psi$ electroproduction off the deuteron. At leading order in the color-octet channels of nonrelativistic QCD, we derive the cross-section contributions associated with longitudinal-longitudinal ($LL$), longitudinal-transverse ($LT$), and transverse-transverse ($TT$) tensor polarization and define ten normalized observables for unpolarized and longitudinally polarized electron beams. Using gluon TMDs obtained in a spin-1 spectator model, we study their $q_T$, $y$, $Q^2$, and collision-energy dependences. The observables involving $f_{1LL}^g$, $f_{1LT}^g+h_{1LT}^g$, and $f_{1TT}^g-h_{1TT}^{\perp g}$ depend directly on ratios of gluon TMDs. The moments involving linearly polarized gluons exhibit a common zero at $Q^2=M_\psi^2$ for the adopted long-distance matrix elements, whereas the beam-helicity-dependent sine moments probe the T-odd distributions $g_{1LT}^g$ and $g_{1TT}^g$. We present fixed-scale model estimates that neglect transverse recoil from soft radiation and quarkonium formation.

papers.title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.

papers.title: Finsler--Sobolev inequalities: optimality & rigidity
papers.abstract: We establish optimal Sobolev and logarithmic-Sobolev inequalities on non-compact, possibly non-reversible Finsler manifolds with non-negative weighted Ricci curvature. The optimal constants exhibit no dependence on reversibility -- confirming Ohta's conjectural principle -- being governed solely by the forward and backward asymptotic volume ratios. We then apply the logarithmic-Sobolev inequality to establish the optimal hypercontractivity estimate for the heat flow in the same geometric setting. The equality cases of the above optimal inequalities imply strong rigidity in the underlying manifold, characterized by fine properties of the flag and $S$-curvatures as well as the precise profiles of the corresponding extremizers. We illustrate our results by examples including Randers metrics obtained by Zermelo navigation with Killing vector fields, and weighted convex cones in $\mathbb{R}^n$ endowed with arbitrary Minkowski norms, the latter showing that the forward and backward asymptotic volume ratios may differ.

papers.title: Neural Schr\"{o}dinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schr\"{o}dinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

papers.title: Control of Underactuated Surface Vessels---Part II: Underway Docking
papers.abstract: In underway directional docking, a second-order nonholonomic problem, six pairs of states of two vehicles have to be made to match by two inputs. The key challenge is to design time-invariant feedback of the relative states and the leader's measured motion only, which makes the follower's convergence in range outpaced, with no sway actuation whatsoever, by the bearing and heading convergence of the follower relative to the leader's path. We begin with nonmodular backstepping, choosing speed and commanded heading jointly to control range and bearing. Curvature compensation and normalization of angular errors by different powers of range remove the range singularity from the model. Our construction passes from unicycle kinematics to the ships' zero-sideslip points and through the sway dynamics to the physical hulls. The design extends to a leader with a different hull and to a docking point astern or abeam of the leader, where we show that, while the leader turns, a follower without sway actuation holds the point only with a heading that differs from the leader's. With strict control Lyapunov construction, we achieve global $\kappa$-exponential convergence, with a rate independent of the initial error.

papers.title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
papers.abstract: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main}{here}.

papers.title: Control of Underactuated Surface Vessels---Part I: Stabilization in Polar Coordinates
papers.abstract: A surface vessel with surge force and yaw moment as inputs and no sway actuation cannot be stabilized at a fixed pose by continuous time-invariant feedback. We introduce a zero-sideslip point, a point whose position relative to the hull depends on the surge and sway speeds and whose velocity points along the vessel's heading at every instant, and show that it moves as a unicycle. This reduction allows the time-invariant, polar-coordinate steering laws of Todorovski et al. (2025) to be applied to the underactuated vessel without modification. With two steering laws, GloBa and BoLSA, we construct strict control Lyapunov functions and prove global asymptotic stability, first for a four-state model with surge speed and yaw rate as virtual inputs, and then, by one step of backstepping, for the full six-state model with surge force and yaw moment. The analysis extends to hulls with fore-aft asymmetric sway-yaw damping, excluded in prior work by the assumption of diagonal damping. Unlike prior time-varying designs, the time-invariant controller yields smooth, non-oscillatory trajectories, an important practical advantage for docking. The designs are validated in simulation on the Cybership I hull model.

papers.title: Rank-unimodality of one-descent composition ideals
papers.abstract: The principal ideal of a composition consists of its distinct generalized subwords, ranked by the sum of their parts. We prove rank-unimodality for every composition with at most one descent and for every bitonic composition. Both the part sizes and the number of parts are unrestricted. The main ingredient is a coupling for a monotone host. If a subword is chosen uniformly among those of weight at most n, its length and its unused weight can be made to increase weakly when n increases by one. A decreasing threshold on the next available part then compares the positive difference of two ordinary rank coefficients with an earlier cumulative ratio. This supplies the coefficient inequality in the hereditary reduction at a strict peak.

papers.title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience
papers.abstract: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.

papers.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
papers.abstract: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

papers.title: Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning
papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)

papers.title: Can Ideologues Agree on Quality? From Non-identifiable Latent Factors to Collective Outcomes
papers.abstract: To surface "objective" fact-check notes, X's Community Notes uses Biased Matrix Factorization (BMF) on crowd-sourced ratings to separate note quality from reviewer ideology. We show that for any correctly specified model that decomposes ratings into quality and ideological alignment, this separation requires fixing an ideological anchor: a reference point for what counts as neutral. We give a characterization for the standard implementation: with $L_2$ regularization, BMF anchors quality at a point proportional to the mean reviewer ideology, recovering objective quality if and only if the mean reviewer is neutral, assuming note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning. This parallels the Condorcet Jury Theorem: collective judgment recovers truth when the pool is unbiased on average. When that assumption fails, BMF's recovered ranking shifts toward maximizing aggregate reviewer satisfaction, which coincides with social welfare only when the pool is representative. This is not specific to BMF; the rating matrix admits a continuous family of gauge-equivalent decompositions, each implying a different quality ranking, so no mechanism based on ratings alone can recover quality without implicitly choosing such an anchor. What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.

papers.title: Deterministic regularisation of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm for pseudospectral shattering in exact arithmetic. This resolves an important open problem in the complexity of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem. Given a complex contraction $A$ of order $n\ge2$ and $0<\delta<1/2$, we compute a perturbation $E$ with $\|E\|<\delta$ such that $A+E$ has simple spectrum. The ratio of its eigenbasis condition number to its minimum eigenvalue gap is at most $C(n/\delta)^{20/3}$. The algorithm also computes an exact eigensystem of $A+E$. It uses $O(n^3\log^d(n/\delta))$ real-field operations and comparisons, where $C$ and $d$ are absolute constants. We choose the rank-one perturbations using a lower bound on the circle mean of the logarithm of the discriminant modulus. A quadratic penalty controls how far the accumulated updates move the matrix. By using the same reference eigenbasis for several updates, we can estimate all the current projector norms while recovering only the directions needed for the next perturbation.

papers.title: Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.

papers.title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange.
