The proof reconstructs the cohomological operator framework for finite $\mathrm{PGL}_3$ quotients from the local link data: the degree operators recover the three determinant factors and together form a cochain map homotopic to multiplication by $1-u^3$. Sylvester's identity gives the resulting alternating determinant relation directly. All constructions use only the finite incidence structure of $X$; no ambient group, field, or building is required.

papers.title: The Rotation Strategy Wins Penney's game for Permutations
papers.abstract: In Penney's game for permutations, two players choose distinct patterns of the same length $k$, and independent random variables with a common continuous distribution are observed until the relative order of $k$ consecutive observations matches one of the patterns; the player who chose that pattern wins. Elizalde and Lin conjectured that the second player wins with probability greater than one half by answering the pattern $a_1a_2\cdots a_k$ with its rotation $a_ka_1\cdots a_{k-1}$. We prove that this conjecture holds for every $k\ge3$. We also show that for $k\ge8$ the rotation wins with probability at least $1/2+0.0053/(k+1)$. The proof writes the advantage of the second player in terms of clusters, which are chains of overlapping marked occurrences of the two patterns weighted by $\pm1$. We show that, for each ordering of the observations, the weights of its clusters sum to $-1$, $0$, or $1$. This gives an explicit bound on the contribution of arbitrarily long clusters, which proves the result analytically for $k\ge8$, and exact rational computations prove it for $3\le k\le7$.

papers.title: Scalability and Performance Trade-offs Between Q-Learning and Parallel Intensified Simulated Annealing in Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
papers.abstract: This article presents a controlled comparison of tabular Q-learning (QL) and Parallelized Simulated Annealing with Intensification (PISA) for the Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP).

papers.title: A Matrix-Valued Quotient and a Compatible Bilinear Product on Euclidean Vector Spaces
papers.abstract: We introduce a matrix-valued quotient and a compatible bilinear product on finite-dimensional Euclidean vector spaces. The quotient is constructed from a bilinear matrix-valued map satisfying a prescribed vector transport identity. We investigate its algebraic structure and establish uniqueness results under orthogonal equivariance and additional structural conditions. We also derive a variational characterization based on the Frobenius norm and examine the spectral properties of the associated matrices, including their determinants and invertibility conditions. The two-dimensional construction is related to complex arithmetic, while the three-dimensional formulation admits a representation using skew-symmetric matrices. The results clarify the relationship between vector transport, matrix algebra, and Euclidean geometry, and extend the framework introduced in our earlier work on vector division and multiplication.

papers.title: Short Paper No. 2: Relations between integer sequences A003622 $\&$ A035336 and two criteria in respect of maximum degrees within the family of finite linear Jaco graphs
papers.abstract: This paper establishes two relationships between integer sequences and the maximum degrees of finite linear Jaco graphs $J_n(x)$. First, it characterizes the positive maximum degrees that occur exactly once within the family, showing that they are generated by the integer sequence A003622. Second, it determines the orders of the corresponding graphs and establishes their relationship with the integer sequence A035336. These results resolve conjectures previously stated in [5]. The proofs were developed with the assistance of AI-based mathematical reasoning technology and subsequently reviewed by the authors.

papers.title: Forsyth--Glaisher-Type Series for $1/\pi$ Involving Catalan Numbers and Harmonic Numbers
papers.abstract: We develop an elementary method for constructing and evaluating families of Forsyth--Glaisher-type series for $1/\pi$. The approach is based on Newton's generalized binomial theorem, identities for generalized binomial coefficients, and Euler's beta integral, together with properties of the gamma and digamma functions. We establish several parameterized identities involving squares of central binomial coefficients and products of odd integers, from which we derive explicit evaluations in terms of $1/\pi$. By means of transformations connecting generalized binomial coefficients with Catalan numbers, we obtain further families of series involving squares of Catalan numbers. We also derive identities for series involving harmonic and odd harmonic numbers by differentiating suitable parameter-dependent formulas. These results yield evaluations containing both $1/\pi$ and logarithmic terms, particularly $\ln 2$. Our results provide a unified framework for generating and evaluating related binomial and Catalan-type series and reveal connections among central binomial coefficients, Catalan numbers, and harmonic numbers.

papers.title: An order on the Leech lattice from a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-symmetric triple-octonion product
papers.abstract: We show that the Leech lattice $\Lambda$ admits the structure of an order in a 24-dimensional real algebra: the lattice is closed under a bilinear product on $\mathbb{R}^{24}$, assembled from nine octonion-multiplication blocks under cyclic $\mathbb{Z}_3$ permutation of three octonion factors. In Robert A. Wilson's sublattice description of $\Lambda$, closure turns on a transposition $\sigma$ of two imaginary basis units: $\sigma$ leaves the $E_8$ lattice $L$ invariant and is an octonion-algebra isomorphism, but moves Wilson's two sublattices of $L$. The proof reduces to four lemmas, three of which follow from the closure of one maximal order of integral octonions. More generally, for every linear map $g$ with $g(L) = L$, the triple product built from the $g$-twisted octonion product closes on $\Lambda$ exactly when Wilson's two sublattices are closed under that product. We determine the idempotents, the square-zero elements, and the automorphism group of the algebra, as well as the automorphism group of the order and the index of the span of its products. We discuss the construction in the context of related work. A historical appendix (1923--1946) traces $\sigma$ to Richard H. Bruck's repair of Johannes Kirmse's integral octonions. The research record of this human--AI collaboration is public.

papers.title: Tearing stability of pulsar equatorial current sheets
papers.abstract: Harris-type current sheets have been studied extensively with particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. These local configurations generally contain no systematic magnetic-field component normal to the current sheet. Such a component develops naturally in a global pulsar magnetosphere because reconnecting field lines connect the northern and southern magnetic hemispheres. We investigate how the normal field component affects the tearing stability and dissipation of the pulsar equatorial current sheet, and we examine the consequences for the global magnetospheric configuration. We combine the tearing-stability condition for a current sheet threaded by a normal field with the electromagnetic relations imposed by the surrounding ideal force-free magnetosphere. We also formulate a dissipative equatorial boundary condition and incorporate it into a global force-free model solved with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). For realistic Lundquist numbers the normal magnetic field can suppress the tearing instability. Preliminary solutions indicate two distinct magnetospheric configurations: a nearly ideal CKF-like state with negligible equatorial dissipation, and a strongly dissipative state resembling the solutions of Contopoulos et al. (2014) and Cerutti et al. (2015). The reconnection rate in the pulsar equatorial current sheet cannot be inferred from local Harris-type current sheet calculations because it depends on the global magnetic topology. Present global 3D PIC simulations operate at effective Lundquist numbers far below astrophysical values, and may therefore exhibit tearing that in a real pulsar magnetosphere would be strongly suppressed.

papers.title: NAVIQUAL-XR: Finding the Sweet Spot of a Live Music Environment in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) enables immersive spatial audio experiences that extend conventional stereo and head-tracked listening to six degrees-of-freedom (6-DoF) navigation. However, evaluating listener Quality of Experience (QoE) remains a key challenge due to the real-time and dynamic adaptations of the content in AR environments. To address this challenge, we propose NAVIQUAL-XR, an objective model to find the "sweet spot" in AR live music environments validated by subjective tests. We recruited 25 listeners who navigated 12 AR environments of various scene set ups under auditory and audio-visual modalities. We analyzed their navigation trajectories and recorded their final locations and directions as their subjective sweet spots. We then produced subjective maps that identified the location and direction with the optimal QoE in an AR environment. Furthermore, we benchmarked key objective metrics that predict these sweet spots through similarity metrics with the subjective maps. We found that localization quality derived from BINAQUAL, an objective metric designed for binaural audio, outperformed signal-to-noise ratio in closely predicting the sweet spot. This suggests that phase-based cues play a more important role on perceived QoE in AR environments than intensity-based cues. NAVIQUAL-XR provides new insights into listener behavior and preferences in AR environments, demonstrating the potential of objective metrics to predict the subjective experience, and guiding the design of future immersive audio systems.

papers.title: SnakeTranslate: Weakly Supervised Policy Learning from Offline Parallel Text for Simultaneous Translation
papers.abstract: Adaptive simultaneous translation requires reliable prefix translation and timely READ/WRITE decisions, but ordinary parallel corpora provide no action annotations. We present SnakeTranslate, which adapts loss-derived alignment to sampled causal histories for jointly learning both capabilities. The framework supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on parallel text and on-policy distillation (OPD) with reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence on student-generated translations. At inference, source and target tokens form one append-only interleaved history, enabling incremental decoding with cache reuse. On FLEURS, NTREX128, and WMT24++, our 4B model improves quality--latency trade-offs over streaming policies applied to the same offline-tuned backbone, with further gains from OPD. It also compares favorably with larger translation models at low and moderate latency, while higher-latency quality gaps remain on WMT24++.

papers.title: Early Evolution of Strange Quark Stars Admixed with Fermionic Dark Matter
papers.abstract: We study strange quark stars admixed with fermionic dark matter (DM) in three quasistatic stages of their early evolution: the neutrino-trapped stage, the heated stage after deleptonization, and the cold stage. Quark matter is described by the MIT bag model at finite temperature with thermal gluons, a repulsive vector interaction, and, in the first stage, trapped neutrinos. The DM is modeled as a cold, asymmetric gas of fermions with masses $m_\chi = 0.3$, $1$, and $3$ GeV, with and without a repulsive self-interaction, and interacts with the quark matter only through gravity. Using the two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, we compute the structure, the maximum masses, and the tidal deformability of the stars in each stage for DM mass fractions $F_D$ up to $5\%$, and we follow individual stars at fixed numbers of baryons and DM particles. The effect of DM is nearly the same in the three stages: for $m_\chi = 1$ GeV and $F_D = 5\%$, DM lowers the maximum mass by about $8\%$ and the tidal deformability of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ star by about $26\%$ in each stage, whereas the stage itself changes these quantities by only a few percent. Heavy DM forms a compact core; for $m_\chi = 3$ GeV without self-interaction, the mass limit of this core can set the maximum mass of the star. Light DM can form an extended halo, which does not increase the maximum mass for the fractions considered. For $m_\chi = 1$ GeV and $F_D = 5\%$, DM lowers the largest baryon mass of a newborn star by about $0.23\,M_\odot$, but this limit increases from the neutrino-trapped to the cold stage in all cases considered, so that DM does not cause a delayed collapse to a black hole. In our model, pulsars of about $2\,M_\odot$ require a stiff quark equation of state and restrict the DM fraction to a few percent unless the DM is light.

papers.title: 5G NR Sensing of Robotic Arm Motion in Indoor Factory Environments
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the performance of monostatic Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems for tracking robotic arm kinematics in industrial factory (InF) environments. Building on a part-specific quasi-deterministic channel model previously derived from high-resolution robotic-arm measurements using our context-aware channel sounder and digital twin, we develop a framework for generating arbitrary articulated motion profiles through hierarchical kinematic transformations. By integrating this high-fidelity target model with the standardized 3GPP InF channel model, we employ 5G New Radio (NR) Positioning Reference Signals (PRS) as the sensing waveform to enable comprehensive system-level evaluation. Simulations are conducted for both sparse clutters (InF-SH) and dense clutters (InF-DH) scenarios using 3GPP-compliant antenna radiation patterns and analog beamforming, allowing us to assess the impact of industrial clutter on sensing performance. The results show that while high estimation accuracy is achievable under Line-of-Sight (LOS) conditions, dense clutter in InF-DH environments introduces severe blockage that significantly limits sensing reliability. In particular, the effective sensing coverage in InF-DH is drastically reduced, with detection probability dropping to approximately \(P_d \approx 10\,\%\) even when the robotic arm is located directly beneath the Transmission Reception Point (TRP). Furthermore, in InF-SH, achieving a high detection probability (e.g., \(P_d \geq 90\,\%\)) requires the target to remain in close proximity to the TRP, with an effective coverage radius of approximately 13 m.

papers.title: Magnetic Reconnection and High-Speed Jets Downstream of a Parallel Shock: Full Particle-in-cell Simulations
papers.abstract: Collisionless shocks are of fundamental interest in astrophysics and space physics as important sources of energetic particles. Downstream of quasi-parallel shocks, high-speed jets (HSJs) and magnetic reconnection have been frequently observed, while it remains unclear how their coupling shapes structured regions for particle energization. We use two-dimensional full particle-in-cell simulations to investigate HSJ generation, thin current sheet formation, and associated electron energization downstream of a parallel shock. We find that portions of foreshock ULF waves with enhanced dynamic pressure interact with a self-reforming shock front and are transmitted downstream, forming HSJs, while neighboring low pressure portions evolve into cavities. At the leading edge of the HSJs, the unique bent magnetic topology carried by the compressed ULF waves produces bow waves and locally squeezes out thin current sheets. These current sheets show reconnection signatures, including X-point topology, magnetic islands, enhanced $J\cdot E'$, and Alfvenic outflows along the local reconnecting direction. In the reconnection region associated with HSJs, the parallel electric field, betatron, and Fermi terms all contribute to adiabatic electron energization. The betatron term appears a visible signature near the X line, where the local magnetic structure is compressed by the HSJ. For the first time, we report a systematic mass-ratio dependence of HSJ morphology in full PIC simulations: lower mass ratios produce fragmented HSJs with shorter lifetimes, whereas larger mass ratios yield longer and wider HSJs with clearer bow waves as ion inertia increases.

papers.title: Critical exponents and spectral functions of totally nonnegative matrices
papers.abstract: We determine the ordinary critical exponent for total positivity. For every oscillatory matrix $A$ of order $n\ge2$, the power $A^t$ is totally positive for $t>n-2$, and this bound is optimal. More generally, if $\psi$ is real and operator monotone on $(0,\infty)$, then $A^\alpha e^{\psi(A)}$ is totally nonnegative for every nonsingular totally nonnegative matrix $A$ of order $n$ when $\alpha\ge n-2$. In this range, if $A$ is oscillatory, the matrix is totally positive when $\alpha>n-2$ or $\psi$ is nonconstant. If $A$ is totally positive and $n\ge4$, every minor of $A^\alpha e^{\psi(A)}$ is positive for $\alpha\ge n-3$ except possibly the $(1,n)$ and $(n,1)$ entries and the two far corners of order $n-1$. In particular, it is a P-matrix. The exponents $t$ for which $A^t$ is a P-matrix for every totally positive matrix $A$ of order $n$ form $\mathbb Z\cup\{t:|t|\ge n-3\}$ for $n\ge4$, and all of $\mathbb R$ for $n\le3$. For $1\le p<n$, the minors of $A^t$ whose row or column set consists of the first or last $p$ indices have sharp tail threshold $\max(p,n-p)-1$ as $A$ ranges over totally positive matrices of order $n$. For a fixed order $n\ge2$, a positive analytic function that preserves nonsingular totally nonnegative matrices maps every oscillatory matrix to a totally positive matrix if and only if it is not a positive multiple of $x^k$ for $k\in\{0,\ldots,n-2\}$.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for English-Swedish Medical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models do well on English medical exams, but less is known about Swedish. This matters most for small open models that hospitals can run locally. To reduce this gap, we first build an item-aligned English-Swedish benchmark from ten medical multiple-choice datasets; each Swedish item keeps the options and answer of its English source. A conservative refinement loop repairs the translations: open models from three families find errors, ground them in a Swedish medical term base, and keep a model-written edit only if blind judges vote for it. On this benchmark, small models lose much more accuracy in Swedish than large ones, especially when they answer without reasoning. Second, we ask whether English data and open teacher models can close this gap. We translate the training data, let teachers write reasoning traces, and fine-tune two small students on gold answers or traces in English, Swedish, or both. Training on reasoning traces that include Swedish closes the gap and lifts the 1.2B student from 23.5\% to 52.0\% in Swedish, slightly above a 20B open model in its fast mode, with a sixth of its memory. We release the benchmark, its edit history, and the code.

papers.title: Foata and Spot Commutation for Parking Functions
papers.abstract: For a parking function $\alpha$, let $\mathrm{spot}(\alpha)$ be the permutation whose $i$th entry is the space occupied by car $i$ and let $\mathrm{foata}(w)$ be Foata's second fundamental transformation on words. Conjecture 6.3 of Celano et al. asserts that $\mathrm{foata}(\mathrm{spot}(\alpha)) = \mathrm{spot}(\mathrm{foata}(\alpha))$ for every unit interval parking function $\alpha$. This paper proves the identity for a larger class: parking functions where each prime component (borrowing Gessel's definition) of $\alpha$ is nondecreasing. Since every unit interval parking function is composed of nondecreasing prime parking functions, the conjecture follows. A key step is showing that $\mathrm{foata}$ preserves the set of parking functions $\alpha$ with $\mathrm{spot}(\alpha) = \mathrm{std}(\alpha)$, where $\mathrm{std}$ denotes standardization. In particular, this proves that inversion count and major index are equidistributed over this larger class.

papers.title: Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards for Human-Behavior Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents in social-science research. A useful simulator should predict individual responses, reproduce population response distributions, and capture demographic differences. Common training approaches struggle to balance these goals: exact-match rewards encourage the model to concentrate on the most frequent human response, which is contradictory to the goal of distributional alignment. Meanwhile, aggregate distribution matching can look good even when demographic information is ignored. To this end, we introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement-learning reward that uses demographic group distribution gaps to guide individual responses, designed by aligning policy generated frequencies with human response frequencies within each question-group margins. We evaluate the method using the OpinionQA dataset and find that comparing with accuracy-only RLVR, DVR preserves per-response accuracy while reducing JSD by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions, with higher DPC point estimates on both splits. Comparing KL-SFT with the demographics-blind marginal further shows that low JSD is insufficient to establish fidelity to population heterogeneity, highlighting that accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure should be evaluated together.

papers.title: Simulation of the oscillation-induced self-propulsion of an immersed body
papers.abstract: We are studying the dynamics of a rigid body that is immersed in an incompressible fluid and exposed to a periodic forcing. The fundamental question is, whether a non-zero average velocity of the body can result, if it is driven by a zero-average force. Recently we have proven exactly such theoretical guarantees for self-propulsion in the case of forces with average zero. This paper is devoted to the numerical simulation of this phenomenon. The problem is non-trivial, as periodic-in-time solutions must be identified to correctly describe the limit dynamics of this coupled problem. Although the body undergoes oscillations with a substantial amplitude the mean velocity will always be smaller by some orders and close to zero. We will derive several acceleration schemes to identify periodic solutions to flow problems. We show numerically the robustness of our scheme with respect to the physical and numerical parameters.

papers.title: Matrix nearness problems via Lie algebra
papers.abstract: As examplified by the Eckart--Young theorem, a matrix nearness problem can be solve by only manipulating only singular values despite having geometrically complicated constraints. In this article, we answer the question of when a matrix nearness problem $D(A,X)$ or $D(X,A)$ can be solved by only manipulating the eigenvalues or singular values of $A$ via the notion of isotropic divergences. We show under an isotropic divergence, a matrix nearness problem with constraints respecting the Lie group symmetry can always be reduced to approximating the eigenvalues or singular values of $A$, providing a systematic way to construct the minimizers. We provide sufficient conditions of isotropy in the classes of Bregman, Jensen, and Calabi's diastasis and verify that a myriad of matrix divergences arising in applications are naturally isotropic, including the Frobenius, von Neumann, logdet, $S$-, quantum Jensen--Shannon, Bures--Wasserstein, quantum Hellinger, and quantum $q$-divergence, among others. This procedure opens the door to for us to construct solutions to a myriad of matrix nearness problems including constraints on rank, spectrum, condition number, trace, determinant, as well as other physically motivated constraints.

papers.title: Quantum Reversal of Dialectics: Inversion of Qualities and Occupation Numbers in Statistical Physics
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual approach to quantum statistics called the inversion of qualities. Inspired by dialectical philosophy and the distinction between quality and quantity, the approach interprets quantum modes as qualitative characteristics and occupation numbers as quantitative measures of their realization. The paper examines the relation between occupation numbers and the statistical behavior of bosons and fermions. It discusses the role of combinatorial reasoning in describing quantum states, the harmonic oscillator, and Planck's black-body radiation formula. The mean occupation number of a bosonic mode is derived using the standard geometric-series method. The approach is compared with the Fock-space formalism and second quantization. Its conceptual scope and limitations are discussed through examples involving electromagnetic modes, phonons, and the hydrogen atom. The proposed inversion is presented as a philosophical interpretation of established quantum-statistical formalism rather than a replacement for standard quantum mechanics.

papers.title: From raw magnetoresistance to reliable cyclotron masses: A practical guide to processing quantum oscillation data
papers.abstract: Quantum oscillations are an essential probe of the Fermi surface in conductors, and cyclotron masses extracted using the Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) formula are used to evaluate correlation strength and the assignment of topological states. These masses depend on choices in signal processing, including the field window, method of background subtraction, and spectral window applied before the Fourier transform. These choices are often guided by visual inspection, yet they can alter spectral features and bias the extracted masses. We show that (1) representing a finite field interval by a single effective field can underestimate the cyclotron mass; (2) polynomial background subtraction can attenuate and shift low-frequency peaks; and (3) spectral tapering can reduce mass bias from leakage between neighboring peaks, at the cost of frequency resolution. We demonstrate these effects using numerical calculations and Shubnikov-de Haas experiments on the rare-earth tritellurides RTe3 (R = Pr, Nd, Gd, Tb) with a dense low-frequency spectrum in the charge ordered state. The examples reveal masses shifting by tens of percent with the field window, apparent peak shifts produced only by the background fit, and a reported departure from LK behavior that resolves into two neighboring frequencies.

papers.title: Dynamic Combinatorics of Quantum Modes in an Inverted Fock Space
papers.abstract: An inversive approach to the combinatorics of Fock space in quantum field theory is proposed. The traditional description of Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac systems is based on distributing indistinguishable quanta (particles) over energy states (modes). The present model introduces a methodological inversion: identical wave modes of a fixed frequency are declared as invariant elements (balls), while discrete occupancy numbers (Fock numbers) act as bins (spatial axes). It is shown that the time evolution of a quantum system governed by elastic interactions represents a trajectory of geometric hops of modes across occupancy axes. This approach eliminates ultraviolet divergences without introducing artificial regulators, visually differentiates thermodynamic quantum statistics, and rigorously derives Planck's entropy and the spectral characteristics of coherent laser systems.

papers.title: Raynaud and Gruson's flattening techniques in Berkovich geometry
papers.abstract: Raynaud and Gruson introduced a flattening procedure for coherent sheaf in the schemes context that rely on sophisticated techniques of algebra and geometry. These methods were later used by Raynaud, Bosch and L\"utkebohmert in formal geometry, and more recently Ducros has developed analogous tools for Berkovich spaces. However, it should be noted that the expression "flattening by blowing up" is, in this context, a little abusive because the flattening process actually requires a succession of blow up and quasi-\'etale morphisms. The aim of this article is to develop a local flattening technique in Berkovich geometry, in the boundaryless case, which only involves blow up.

papers.title: Approximation by classical summability methods in variable Lebesgue spaces
papers.abstract: We investigate approximation by Fej\'er and N\"orlund means with respect to the Walsh system in variable Lebesgue spaces. We prove that the Fej\'er means are uniformly bounded on the weighted space $L^1_w[0,1)$ if and only if $w\in A_1(\mathcal{D})$. We then apply Rubio de Francia extrapolation to show that both means are uniformly bounded on $L^{p(\cdot)}[0,1)$ with $1\le p_-\le p_+<\infty$ if and only if $p(\cdot)\in\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})$. Finally, we estimate the approximation errors via the modulus of smoothness and deduce convergence rates for variable Lipschitz classes.

papers.title: On the Sensitivity of Fermi-LAT Maximum Likelihood Stacking
papers.abstract: Stacking sub-threshold gamma-ray sources has become common practice for understanding high-energy emission processes at the population level. In this procedure, one co-adds log-likelihood ratios, called TS values (TS = 2ln$(L_1/L_0)$), for a source class of interest. It is best practice to compare the population of sub-threshold targets against a population of control field test sources (CFs) selected to represent the unmodeled \gray\ background. Determining the significance of a TS measurement stack has typically been difficult. In this work, we find the necessary cumulative TS value ($\Sigma$TS) of a sub-threshold population of $N$ targets to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation from a like-sized population of CFs. We find that the $\Delta (\Sigma$TS) needed to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation is $\sim 70$. In taking this measurement, we characterize the source distribution corresponding to the measured $\Sigma$TS for a significantly detected stack and even predict new individual source detections in larger stacks.

papers.title: Lusin and pseudo-Lusin theorems for monotone measures: necessary conditions, conjugate duality and a correction of a theorem of Castaldo and Marinacci
papers.abstract: Lusin's theorem for monotone measures has been studied mainly through sufficient conditions. Here we study it from the side of necessary conditions and of conjugate duality. We show that, for an arbitrary monotone measure on a metric space, the Lusin property with closed sets implies regularity, and the Lusin property with compact sets implies order continuity and tightness. Consequently, for finite submeasures the Lusin property is characterized by order continuity on compact spaces, and the compact-set Lusin property is characterized by order continuity on Polish spaces. We then consider a pseudo-Lusin property, in which the Lusin set is required to have almost full measure, and observe that it is exactly the Lusin property of the conjugate measure. For finite monotone measures whose conjugate is subadditive, a class including supermodular capacities, belief functions and coherent lower probabilities, the pseudo-Lusin property is equivalent to continuity from below on compact spaces, and so is its compact-set version on Polish spaces. As an application, we give a corrected form, together with its converse, of a Lusin-type theorem of Castaldo and Marinacci whose original statement was refuted by Wiesel. Several examples, one of them based on meagre sets, show that the hypotheses cannot be omitted.

papers.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs
papers.abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

papers.title: Photomeson-threshold origin of the TeV break in astrophysical neutrinos: Spectrum, flavor, resolved sources, and the ultrahigh-energy landscape
papers.abstract:
IceCube observes a break near 30 TeV in the diffuse astrophysical neutrino spectrum. We interpret it as the photomeson ($p\gamma$) threshold. Accelerated protons interact with the soft x rays of accreting black holes through the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance. One kinematic relation sets the break energy from the target field's lowest photon energy, the seed scale $\varepsilon_0$. The measured break fixes $\varepsilon_0\simeq0.13$ keV and supplies the low-energy suppression no sum of falling power laws can produce. Building on the $\Delta(1232)$ identification of Khatee Zathul, Fang, Halzen, and Hooper and the single-source-class photo-pion fit of Winter, Fiorillo, and Buson, we give closed-form relations that invert the four broken-power-law parameters to the source physics with no remaining freedom, namely, $\gamma_2=s$ and $\gamma_1=s-(\alpha_x-1)$ ($s$, $\alpha_x$ the proton and target photon indices), and $E_{m br}\propto[(1+ ar z)\varepsilon_0]^{-1}$. The break width bounds the total smearing to $\sigma_s\le0.235$ dex (68% CL), no broader than redshift alone must make it, and the seed scale is the same across sources to within a factor $\lesssim$1.5, which mean-spectrum fits do not provide. Below-break neutrinos are predicted to come on average from higher redshifts than those above. The threshold also fixes the flavor and $
u/ ar
u$ composition, including the energy-dependent $ ar
u_e$ fraction and the Glashow-resonance discriminator of Winter et al., matching current flavor data. Inverted source by source, the relation gives each resolved IceCube source its target photon scale, from the keV coronae of NGC 1068 and PKS 1424+240 to the $\sim$20 eV jet of TXS 0506+056. That two-decade spread means they cannot supply the homogeneous break, which requires a separate, fainter population. KM3-230213A points to a warm-dust target, $\varepsilon_0\simeq0.02$ eV, unless cosmogenic.

papers.title: Strain-transfer at the Cu nanoparticle-Si(111) interface: static atomistic modelling and simulated Bragg CDI
papers.abstract: Substrate strain offers a route to control deformation in supported metallic nanoparticles, provided that interfacial coupling transmits the imposed loading into the particle. We assess this feasibility using five static Cu/Si(111) configurations spanning 0-2% biaxial tensile substrate strain. A 211,288-atom Cu particle is supported by a nominally 50 x 50 x 20 nm Si slab with its bottom 1 nm fixed, using the Jelinek modified embeddedatom potential. Relative to the relaxed supported 0% state, Cu-only local fits reveal heterogeneous, anisotropic deformation: particle-wide mean hydrostatic strain is negative at every nonzero loading, from -3.12 x 10-6 to -8.84 x 10-6, while the upper-particle mean varies nonmonotonically. Simulated Bragg CDI of Cu(111), obtained by inversion of known complex atomic scattering amplitudes, maps loading-dependent projected displacement and strain. The combined atomistic and Bragg CDI representations provide strong preliminary support for the feasibility of substrate-mediated strain transfer in this idealized system and identify spatial signatures for experimental investigation. Experiments remain indispensable to confirm transfer in real Cu/Si(111) nanoparticles and determine its magnitude.

papers.title: Making Reconnection Cooler: A relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics model for radiative collisionless reconnection
papers.abstract: Relativistic magnetic reconnection around astrophysical compact objects is a likely site for particle energization and multiwavelength emission. Kinetic theory has substantially modelled such collisionless radiative relativistic reconnection using a radiative drag force countering the acceleration of the particles. Here, we systematically derive an energy-momentum sink term in relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics (RRMHD), informed by kinetic theory and coupled with a charge-starved resistivity prescription which reproduces the fast reconnection rate seen in kinetic calculations, to model radiative losses. We show that our radiative loss term accurately captures important macroscopic properties -- including the temperature in the reconnection layer and the bulk motion energy distribution of the out-flowing plasma -- for inverse Compton cooling applied to two-dimensional RRMHD simulations of a reconnection layer and benchmarked to kinetic simulations. Our results hold in various cooling regimes with a one-to-one mapping to kinetic theory. Our radiative model lays a foundation for future RRMHD simulations of plasma in the relativistic radiative regime, such as in reconnection sites in a local turbulent flow or globally in the magnetospheres of black holes and neutron stars.

papers.title: Distributed Multimodal Monitoring and Prediction for PV Asset and Site Conditions
papers.abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) monitoring remains fragmented: electrical performance, structural condition and vegetation management are typically assessed through separate workflows, making it difficult to relate changes in energy performance to the local physical and environmental conditions experienced by individual modules. We propose a distributed multimodal monitoring and prediction framework that combines mechanical, optical, electrical, and microclimate measurements at the string level. Rather than treating these measurements as independent sensor streams, the framework uses them to derive higher-level indicators of asset and site condition, including quantities that are not directly instrumented. We designed and installed four compact wireless nodes attached directly to the rear of PV modules for a three-month pilot study to demonstrate module-level monitoring. From low-cost multimodal measurements, the system detected vegetation-management events, predicted wind speed from module vibration on unseen data, and extracted repeatable structural-frequency fingerprints associated with individual module locations. These preliminary results demonstrate a pathway from distributed monitoring toward predictive PV asset management, where multimodal observations can be used to predict or estimate otherwise unobserved operating and structural states, identify emerging changes earlier, and provide more granular intelligence than plant-level electrical monitoring or periodic inspection alone.

papers.title: WISP: Composable Representations for Wrist-Worn Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Smartwatches and fitness bands are among the most common wearable devices, and large national health studies record movement at the wrist. Yet existing human activity recognition benchmarks mix sensors worn on different parts of the body, so they do not show how well activities can be recognised from the wrist alone. We introduce WristHARBench, a benchmark that standardises participant-disjoint evaluation across nine wrist-acceleration datasets and two additional multichannel inertial datasets. We hypothesise that different human activities leave complementary patterns in wrist motion, such as local shape, rhythm, temporal order and cross-axis relationships, and propose WISP (Wrist-Informed Space of Predictive Representations), a composable representation space that combines representations of these patterns with compatible classifiers. Across the nine primary datasets, WISP with random search achieves 70.20% mean Macro-F1, compared with 59.62% for the strongest of 18 external baselines. Controlled ablations and baseline comparisons indicate that recognition improves mainly when a representation adds motion patterns that the others lack, rather than when it represents the same pattern in a different way.

papers.title: Choosing a Side is not Enough: Epistemic Transparency Under Knowledge Conflict
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in professional knowledge work, where their outputs can influence decisions with real-world consequences. When a model encounters information that contradicts its prior knowledge, it should communicate this conflict transparently to the user. Existing work on knowledge conflicts focuses on which source, parametric or contextual, a model chooses, rather than whether models disclose the presence of the conflict. Moreover, existing work primarily studies multiple-choice questions under simplified counterfactual evidence generation schemes. In this work, we address the first gap by scoring model responses against a taxonomy of epistemic transparency, rather than measuring accuracy alone. We address the second gap by proposing a general framework for generating knowledge conflicts grounded in advanced domain knowledge, which we instantiate in this work as a set of real-world tasks based on counterfactual evidence. These contributions allow us to measure epistemic transparency under realistic knowledge conflicts, as well as the impact of the format and plausibility of the evidence, and the real-world stakes of the task. We find substantial differences in transparency across five evaluated frontier models, with none fully matching our definition of optimal, risk-sensitive epistemic alignment. We hope that our work will ground future discussion of epistemic transparency in real-world applications of LLMs, and help establish a risk framework for epistemic transparency across domains and deployment scenarios.

papers.title: Corrigendum to "Well-posedness and regularity of the integral invariant model from linear scalar transport equation" [J. Math. Anal. Appl. 564 (2026) 130904]
papers.abstract: We clarify the compactly supported terminal test space and the moving-domain Bochner spaces in the integral invariant formulation. We complete the existence proof by establishing strong measurability and the initial trace, and replace the stability argument by a compact-test density argument that retains the original stability constant. A short appendix shows that the integral invariant identity remains valid for all square-integrable terminal test functions that vanish almost everywhere outside the terminal domain, thereby admitting the zero extensions of the cell polynomials used in the SLDG/SLFV method. We also correct the velocity and divergence in the swirling-deformation example.

papers.title: DRU-Mixer: An Explainable Dilated Recurrent Unit-Based Mixer Model with Focal Loss for EEG-Based Interictal Epileptiform Discharges Detection
papers.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges (IED) have been identified as a core electroencephalogram (EEG) biomarker in diagnosing epilepsy patients. However, automatic detection and classification of IED require significant effort by human experts and can be prone to inter-rater variability. This paper presents Dilated Recurrent Units (DRU)-Mixer, a deep learning network to automate the process of identifying and classifying IED based on EEG recordings. The proposed architecture comprises a convolutional front end for extracting local features, dilated recurrent units modeling the temporal relationship between EEG signals, and mixer modules for token- and channel-level representation learning. DRU-Mixer was trained to perform (i) binary classification of IED/Non-IED segments and (ii) multiclass classification of regional IED types. For binary classification, DRU-Mixer showed 95.19% accuracy, 72.76% precision, 82.31% recall, 96.61% specificity, and 77.24% F1-score. For multiclass classification, the proposed network achieved strong sensitivity between 74.8% and 89.2%, as well as precision between 70.5% and 86.3%. Sensitivity-oriented analysis of the results shows that, for 70% sensitivity, DRU-Mixer provided 83.8% precision and 98.5% specificity outperforming VGGEEG and VGGSleep models and being on par with vEpiNet model. Interpretability of the model's results was estimated through occlusion mapping technique, which was used to highlight time intervals and EEG channels providing maximal contribution to the prediction. Maps generated by the technique show specific patterns for IED and Non-IED indicating that the model utilizes structured channel-time features corresponding to the presence of epileptiform activity.

papers.title: Safety Systems Watch What the Model Says, Not What the Child Says
papers.abstract: Children are increasingly talking to consumer chatbots. We audit the published category definitions of 17 safety taxonomies and child-safety benchmarks. Combinations of these systems lead us to 144 categories whose definitions could be reliably coded: 104 classify properties of model output, 25 classify user intent, and 15 describe user-state or user-impact. Within these 15 user-state/user-impact categories, 10 attribute the relevant condition to the system, 1 to the user, 2 concern the user's disclosure of personal information, and 2 do not specify the responsible source. None of the coded categories identifies harm inflicted on the child by another person as the object of evaluation. Child abuse appears repeatedly across these taxonomies, but as prohibited content, prohibited generation, or prohibited user intent, not as an externally inflicted condition that a child may disclose to the model. Consequently, a child reporting abuse has no dedicated taxonomy label that identifies the disclosure as a safety-relevant event requiring a response distinct from content suppression. We ran five behavioural probes, grounded in the child-disclosure literature, through six publicly accessible consumer-facing chat models to examine the behavioural consequences of this omission. We propose no detection system. Instead, we prove that externally inflicted harm disclosed to an AI system remains unnamed in the evaluation vocabulary used by current safety taxonomies, and that naming the missing case is a precondition for measuring, comparing, and improving model behaviour toward such disclosures.

papers.title: A Data-Mining Approach to Library User Segmentation: Clustering Readers by Perceived Marketing Communication
papers.abstract: This paper applies unsupervised data mining to segment users of information-library centers by their perception of digital and marketing communication. The empirical basis is a survey of readers from fifteen information-library centers in Uzbekistan. From 213 responses, 180 complete records with seven Likert-scale perception variables were retained. After z-score standardization, k-means clustering was used, and the number of clusters was selected by the silhouette coefficient with additional validation by the Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin indices. A stable four-cluster solution was obtained: Engaged Enthusiasts, Moderately Satisfied, Loyal-in-spite-of and Disengaged. The main finding is a perception-loyalty paradox: some users remain satisfied even when mediated communication is weakly perceived. The proposed segmentation provides a reproducible instrument for differentiated communication planning in library management.
authors: Martin V. Grebenyuk (Uzbekistan State Institute of Arts

papers.title: A No-Code Toolchain for Validating Wearable Motion Sensing Systems
papers.abstract: Designing e-textiles for human motion sensing often demands engineering expertise for sensor data processing, typically relying on advanced machine learning methods. In addition, validating designs---collecting sensor measurements and ground-truth motion data, training and testing machine learning models, and iterating on sensor layouts---can be labour- and time-intensive. To address this, we present a no-code toolchain that enables non-technical users to validate system designs efficiently. The tool provides three key capabilities: (1) deriving ground-truth joint-angle measurements from webcam recordings; (2) training and testing machine learning models using collected sensor data; and (3) visualising and analysing motion sensing performance and sensor layout choices. Our tool requires a simple, low-cost setup and produces test reports within minutes. A user study was conducted to validate the usability of this toolchain. This toolchain is open source and available at https://github.com/yaozhang182/etextile-validation-gui.

papers.title: REMORA: A Voice-First Memory Assistant for Grounded Personal Recall and Independent Living
papers.abstract: Most of what matters in a day is spoken and written down nowhere: a dosing interval named at a clinic, a deadline moved in passing, the place a document was set down. Such information is consequential because it is operational, and fragile because it arrives during divided attention -- the moment its importance becomes clear is rarely the moment it was said. For people living with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease or age-related episodic memory decline, that gap bounds independent living. Conventional aids close it poorly: notes, reminders and calendars require the user to notice, interrupt and transcribe, adding extraneous cognitive load exactly where attention is already committed. We present REMORA, a voice-first memory assistant that converts consented speech into structured, auditable memory records. REMORA transcribes and diarizes captured audio, extracts memory candidates -- tasks, appointments, names, instructions, object locations -- each retaining provenance into the conversation it came from, and holds records, embeddings and relationships in a single relational system of record. Recall combines lexical, semantic, relational and recency signals, since no one signal covers the ways people interrogate their own past, and reaches the user either through an explicit query or through a confidence-gated cue that stays silent unless it is likely to help. Generation is bound by a grounding contract: only retrieved evidence may be used, and absent a supporting memory REMORA abstains rather than confabulates, because a fluent invention about one's own past will be acted upon as fact. A requirements survey and a pilot study with memory-loss users indicate that conversational forgetting extends well beyond clinical populations, that grounded and concise recall is feasible in controlled settings, and that privacy, rather than accuracy, is the binding constraint on adoption.

papers.title: Measuring Human-AI and AI-AI Teams in Multi-turn Layout Creation
papers.abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.

papers.title: Do Simulated Users Push Back Like Real Users? Correctness vs. Stance
papers.abstract: LLM-simulated users stand in for people in multi-turn evaluations, on the assumption that they react to what the assistant says. We test this for pushback. From WildChat, we take conversations in which the assistant explicitly challenges or endorses a position the user stated, and compare the real next user turn with simulated turns from the same prefix. Among users who replied, real users push back more after a challenge than after an endorsement (20.5% vs. 8.2%); a GPT-based simulator does not (27.1% vs. 27.1%): stance gap D = -0.12 [-0.17, -0.08]. After a challenge the simulator instead often re-states or re-interprets its request ("I meant ..."); about half of these turns are disguised insistence, which puts D between -0.08 and -0.05. What drives the simulator's disputing is whether the assistant's position is judged correct (21% vs. 49% after challenges; 16% vs. 58% after endorsements), while real users change little (19% vs. 24%; 7% vs. 12%), under every outcome definition we tried. Real same-stance examples do not fix this, and another GPT-based simulator and two Claude simulators show stance effects close to real users. Stance sensitivity should be measured for each simulator, not assumed.

papers.title: Integrating a one-dimensional convolutional neural network with nonlinear model predictive control for slug flow modeling and control
papers.abstract: Severe slugging in pipeline--riser systems degrades production efficiency and threatens equipment integrity, motivating the development of accurate yet deployable control models. This paper presents a lightweight, data-driven modeling and control framework specifically designed for slug flow. First, we revisit a commonly used low-order mechanistic model and introduce two changes that improve physical plausibility and numerical robustness: (i) an explicit zero-outflow boundary during the starvation period at the riser top, and (ii) a reformulated expression for the liquid volume fraction at the riser top that enforces admissible bounds. Synthetic input--output trajectories generated by this model are then used to train a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN) that parameterizes a neural ODE with an affine-in-control. Training employs an 8-step free-roll objective on standardized data; a differential sensitivity check confirms an explicit control channel. The learned model is embedded in a shooting-based nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) scheme with bounded and rate-smoothed actuation. In closed-loop simulations at {\Delta}t = 0.1 second, the controller drives the output to a constant setpoint within approximately 15--18 seconds while maintaining smooth, bounded inputs and non-oscillatory transients. The results indicate that a simple 1D CNN, coupled with NMPC, can capture the characteristic oscillations and regime transitions of slug flow and deliver effective regulation with modest computational cost. Although training is conducted offline to ensure reproducibility, the architecture and identification procedure are designed for extension to online learning, providing a practical path toward adaptive slug-flow mitigation.

papers.title: FittedGenes: Domain-Aware Sewing Pattern Layout Optimization
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional cutting and packing problems aim to arrange pieces on a larger surface without overlap while minimizing material waste. Although extensively studied in industries such as textiles, traditional nesting research assumes piece geometries are fixed. In this work, we make the garment design itself a variable of the nesting optimization: we introduce a new formulation of the sewing pattern nesting problem in which panel geometry is modified under domain-aware constraints, preserving fit while allowing appearance to vary within designer-set bounds. We present an evolutionary nesting framework that embeds these modifications directly into a genetic algorithm (GA). Two novel mutation operators are proposed: one enables splitting panels into stitchable sub-panels, and the other adjusts garment design while preserving fit. Our method is evaluated on existing irregular nesting benchmarks and a new benchmark derived from a comprehensive dataset of sewing patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that evolutionary algorithms enhanced with the proposed garment-aware mutations achieve markedly better results than versions restricted to standard permutation-based operators, demonstrating the value of integrating design flexibility into nesting optimization. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/fittedgenes/GarmentCode-Nesting.

papers.title: Characterization and Monte Carlo Simulation of Wavelength-Shifting Absorption Length in Plastic Optical Fibers
papers.abstract: We report an experimental characterization of the wavelength-shifting (WLS) absorption length of the EJ-160I fiber core material from Eljen Technology. Fiber-core samples of different thicknesses were employed, and the transmitted intensity of incident LED light was measured to extract the WLS absorption length at 405.7 nm. The resulting value, (0.823 +/- 0.038) mm, was used to normalize the WLS absorption length spectrum derived from the absorption spectrum of the core material. An independent measurement at 392.5 nm yielded a WLS absorption length of (1.404 +/- 0.074) mm, differing from the value predicted by the reconstructed WLS absorption length spectrum by 3.16%, corresponding to 0.43 sigma. The resulting spectrum was implemented as an optical input in a Geant4-based optical Monte Carlo simulation of the EJ-160I fiber to examine the role of the WLS absorption length in light output, light attenuation, and the emission spectrum.

papers.title: SoundFleXR: Selectively Constraining Axes of Audio Rendering Presentations
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) systems increasingly rely on audio cues to help users locate, interpret, and interact with virtual content, especially when the content is outside the field of view. To support this, many systems use head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) to approximate real-world acoustics. However, a realistic simulation is only one possible presentation. Audio can also be altered by constraining, flexing, or contracting the spatial dimensions represented in the signal. This work examines how selectively constraining or flexing the number of audio dimensions affects localization performance across XR task structures with different spatial degrees of freedom. We compare two-channel spatial audio, azimuth-only HRTF, and full HRTF rendering across orientation-based (3DoF) and translation-based (6DoF) tasks. Azimuth-only HRTF was mutually non-inferior to full HRTF for total angular error across task conditions, including at the strictest tested tolerance in 3DoF (5 degrees), and remained comparable for azimuth error at (10 degrees) and larger tolerances in both 3DoF and 6DoF. In contrast, two-channel stereo required coarser tolerances to reach non-inferiority, becoming comparable to full HRTF for 6DoF azimuth error at (15 degrees) but not (10 degrees). From these comparisons, we derive design lessons and application scenarios that indicate when fewer spatial cues provide sufficient support and when richer spatial cues are beneficial.

papers.title: Light Shining Through the Moon: A Lunar-Occultation Helioscope for Solar Axions
papers.abstract: We propose a lunar-occultation helioscope in which the Moon suppresses the direct solar x-ray beam before solar axions enter the terrestrial magnetosphere, where they may reconvert into keV photons. We evaluate the conversion with a geomagnetic model combining the IGRF-14 internal contribution and the Tsyganenko T89 external magnetospheric contribution, retaining the two signed transverse components in the oscillation amplitude. As an explicit realizability test, we propagate a circular near-600-km polar orbit through the 12 August 2026 occultation. A $4'$-radius region around the solar center remains lunar occulted for about $470$ s while the sunward line of sight stays clear of the Earth; the coherent magnetic lever arm spans $69.1$--$96.4~\mathrm{T\,m}$ with $\mathcal I_{B,\mathrm{rms}}=76.9~\mathrm{T\,m}$. A B16-AGSS09 Primakoff calculation shows that this aperture contains $97.4\%$ of the 3--15 keV axion flux. For an explicitly specified NuSTAR-like detector benchmark, the propagated single-event exposure gives an expected low-mass 95\% C.L. sensitivity of $g_{a \gamma}=1.31\times10^{-10}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. The proposal therefore establishes the plausibility of a distinct experimental channel for solar-axion searches, characterized by a lunar-defined spatial and temporal window and by a predictable geomagnetic modulation. A future detection would additionally provide directional access to the axion-emitting solar core, opening a complementary probe of the solar interior.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Small-System A/B Trials: Detecting Differences in Newsletter Engagement
papers.abstract: Good experimental practice and predicting the scientific usefulness of an experiment or experimental platform require power analysis: estimating, *a priori*, how likely the experiment is to detect the intended effect if indeed it exists. While simple experimental designs admit well-understood power analysis methods, more sophisticated experimental designs and settings often require bespoke techniques to avoid either over- or under-estimating experimental power. We present the Monte Carlo method we use to estimate the power of experiments intended to increase user engagement with personalized e-mail newsletters of recommended news articles.

papers.title: When Modalities (Dis)Agree: How Decomposing Multi-Modal AI Advice Shapes Appropriate Reliance
papers.abstract: Multi-modal AI systems integrate diverse data streams into unified advices, but this fusion conceals how individual modalities contribute to the final output. Consequently, decision-makers cannot observe whether underlying sources aligned or contradicted one another when assessing the provided advice. To test whether revealing this structure supports appropriate reliance, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (N = 240) in which participants evaluated used-car prices with multi-modal AI support. In a 2x2 between-subjects design, we varied the disclosure of modality-level outputs and natural-language explanations, crossed with within-subjects modality agreement. Revealing modality-level outputs increased reliance, while explanations improved decision accuracy independently. However, this occurred only when modalities agreed: visible consensus acted as a persuasive cue that generally amplified adherence, rather than helping participants override errors under conflict. Thus, decomposing multi-modal advice can make AI advice more persuasive without making errors easier to detect.

papers.title: Cultural and Regional Influences on Global AI Apprehension
papers.abstract: The discussion surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) is primarily influenced by Western viewpoints, often neglecting the cultural, regional, and socio-political factors that affect global perceptions of AI. This study examines how these factors shape AI apprehension in various regions, including Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. A qualitative literature review was conducted, analyzing peer-reviewed articles, policy reports, and gray literature from multiple regions. The study used a comparative approach to assess the cultural, political, and economic contexts shaping AI perceptions. It found significant regional differences in AI concerns: Western countries emphasize privacy, surveillance, and ethics, while regions like Africa and Asia focus on technological dependency, state control, and socio-economic issues, such as job displacement. Brazil and Argentina were noted for their AI governance models, while South Africa and Kenya leverage AI to tackle socio-economic challenges. The findings underscore the need for inclusive AI governance frameworks that respect diverse local contexts and values. These frameworks would contribute to a better understanding of AI's global impact and inform future policy development.

papers.title: Misalignment Between Educators' Testing and End Users' Behavior: What 17,000+ Chatbot Messages Reveal About AI Literacy Training for Teachers
papers.abstract: AI literacy training for educators is expanding rapidly, but its effectiveness rests largely on self-report, knowledge tests, or interviews, revealing little about whether learning carries into practice or affects students and colleagues who use what educators build. We implemented AI for Learning, an asynchronous online course that trained 87 higher-education educators to recognize AI's capabilities, limitations, and ethics; apply prompt engineering; and evaluate AI outputs. Its central assignment asked educators to build, test, and voluntarily deploy chatbots for their practice on an educational chatbot authoring platform. Using LLM-assisted qualitative coding validated against human annotation, we analyzed the resulting 214 chatbots and their builder-bot, peer-bot, and end user-bot conversations, 17,000+ messages spanning 1.5 years. Educators 1) specified what bots should do more often than what they should not; 2) adopted templated prompt components but rarely untemplated strategies; and 3) tested routine use but seldom iterated, leaving 74% of end users' adversarial use untested. Still, 36 bots (17%) reached end users and 63 (29%) were adopted by peers. We contribute two successes and two lessons spanning the lifecycle of educator AI literacy training.

papers.title: Spectral evolution and secular shift of the Z source GX 340+0: an interpretation in the spreading layer paradigm
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive spectral and timing study of the bright neutron star low-mass X-ray binary and Z source, GX 340+0, using broadband X-ray observations with AstroSat in 2020 and 2024, focusing on the evolution of physical parameters along the Z track and the origin of secular shifts of this track across different epochs. The spectra are consistently described by the same model, comprising blackbody emission from a spreading boundary layer near the neutron star surface, an accretion disk, and a Comptonizing corona. We observe a significant decrease in the blackbody temperature from ~1.2 keV on the horizontal branch (HB) to ~1.0 keV on the normal branch (NB), which likely contributes to the harder spectra on the HB and softer spectra on the NB. At the same time, the blackbody normalization varies substantially from ~440-860, indicating changes in the effective emitting area. Within the spreading layer framework, this evolution reflects changes in the extent of theradiating layer, while the large absolute normalization values suggest an additional contribution from the boundary layer. We also detect variations in the absorption column density, suggesting structural changes in the inner accretion disk, possibly linked to radiation driven puffing-up. The Comptonized flux shows a branch-dependent behavior, remaining relatively stable along the HB but decreasing along the NB. We interpret these results within a unified framework where the boundary layer, corona, and inner disk evolve coherently with accretion rate, explaining both the Z-track behavior and its secular shifts.

papers.title: Do as I Say, Not as You Do: Assessing Public Versus Practitioner Perspectives on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Language Technologies
papers.abstract: With the public awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications such as large language models (LLMs) and generative text-to-video models reaching unprecedented levels, there is an increasing need to reconcile the perspectives held by informed practitioners, who research and develop these technologies, with the interests and opinions of the general public, who constitute the majority of people impacted by technological developments. In this work, we survey practitioners (i.e., academics and industry professionals) alongside members of the general public on perspectives relating to pertinent areas of artificial intelligence, including perceived benefit and risk, the ability for models to achieve consciousness and output art, and the use of copyright protected material for model training. Alongside comparisons of diverse perspectives on these topics, we additionally contextualise the findings with a discussion of relevant literature that supports and refutes the myriad observed stances.

papers.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic Human-AI Collaboration: Foundations, Conceptual Framework, and Applications
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across workplaces and industries, ranging from manufacturing plants to healthcare facilities, has paved the way to the design of systems in which humans and AI collaborate on shared tasks. The first developments of Human-AI Collaboration (HAIC) were driven by advances in Machine Learning (ML), which enabled the automation of numerous tasks, including large-scale data processing, image analysis, and speech recognition. However, ML automation have proven insufficient for certain applications due to methodological, safety, and ethical concerns. In such cases, researchers argue for integrating human expertise into operational workflows to improve performance, relying on the complementary skill sets of humans and AI. Despite long-standing research, the field of HAIC has not yet reached full maturity, largely due to the intrinsic difficulty of ensuring a seamless communication between humans and AI. This challenge is partially addressed by Explainable AI methods, which aim to make internal model reasoning more transparent through human-understandable explanations. Recognizing the need for a shared interface between humans and AI in collaborative settings, we propose a novel conceptual framework, NeSy-HAIC, that leverages Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy AI) to bridge the semantic gap between machine representations and human-understandable symbolic concepts. The framework builds on current research in NeSy AI and HAIC, supports multiple interaction paradigms, including Human-In-The-Loop and Human-On-The-Loop, and is characterized through its enabling methodologies and two illustrative use cases in semi-autonomous driving and security alert prioritization. We argue that the integration of data-driven learning and symbolic reasoning can substantially enhance human-AI interaction and mitigate limitations of collaborative systems.

papers.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
papers.abstract: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

papers.title: Evaluating the Participation of Proactive Scouting Agents in Real-time Human Team Meetings
papers.abstract: An open research question is whether the addition of conversational AI agents to real-time discussions among human teams enhances group performance. This study tested the value of adding proactive scouting agents to teams engaged in collaborative forecasting tasks. These agents were designed to (i) monitor the groupwise discussion in real-time, (ii) identify critical information gaps in the group deliberation, (iii) autonomously find and retrieve relevant information, and (iv) express the acquired content into the conversation using emulated groupwise human etiquette. In a controlled set of trials, small human teams of 4 or 5 members were tasked with collaboratively predicting the outcome of 34 Major League Baseball (MLB) games, either by forecasting the winning team or by predicting the total number of runs scored. In half the trials, the groups were assisted by proactive scouting agents. The other half were human-only deliberations. When tasked with predicting the winning team, the addition of proactive scouting agents to the group discussion significantly increased forecasting accuracy, reducing the predictive mean-absolute error by 25% (p=0.006) and improving raw predictive accuracy from 60.0% to 76.4% (p=0.050). When predicting the total number of runs scored across both teams, the addition of proactive scouting agents yielded no statistical change in group performance. It should be noted that the human participants in this study were significantly worse at predicting the number of runs scored. This may have led to random outcomes in those forecasting trials. Still, the results of this study demonstrate that deploying proactive scouting agents can significantly boost forecasting accuracy during real-time team deliberations when participants possess baseline forecasting skill.

papers.title: Psychological State Monitoring Methods Based on Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: The computer-Based Multimodal Emotion Recognition System needs to increase the accuracy and reliability of psychological state monitoring. A hierarchical framework was proposed in this paper to integrate facial images, speech signals and other physiological indicators of emotion in time and space for more complete analysis of human emotions. Synchronously sample data streams from webcams, microphones and wearable sensors, and then preprocess and extract features specific to each type of data. A high-end fusion architecture is adopted to combine early- and late-fusion methods and thus robustly integrate cross-modal information. Experimental validation in a real-world stress-response dataset showed good performance. The overall recognition accuracy and mean F1-score of the fused multimodal system are both about 91% and 0.88, respectively, which are superior to the best unimodal approach (face, 88% accuracy and F1-score 0.88). Temporal analysis shows that the groups for stress tracking are not uniformly adapted and resilient, and ablation experiments have determined which modules contribute significantly to the stability of the system. According to all kinds of quantitative evaluations of precision, recall, accuracy and F1 scores, the proposed method shows good balance and is practical and generally applicable. The research has provided an engineering-feasible, data-driven solution for precise emotion inference and offered methodological support for intelligent mental health assessment and human-centered system design.

papers.title: The Agent Is Not Your Driver: Clarifying the Implied Capabilities of In-Vehicle Anthropomorphic Agents
papers.abstract: This position paper considers how the gap between an anthropomorphic agent in an autonomous vehicle and the automated driving system of the vehicle can create psychological risks if the agent inaccurately presents itself as integrated into the driving system. This gap is under-explored both because of the evolving nature of these agents and because of study limitations in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research. Nevertheless, this gap may cause the agent to misrepresent itself as more knowledgeable about the car than it is, creating a risk of dependence and, in the worst case, betrayal if the occupant feels that the agent has misled them. This paper proposes a research agenda for future work to understand the psychological risk that exists in the gap between agents and driving systems and to narrow this gap in a manner aligned with safety assurance. As these agents evolve to hold greater capabilities and increased anthropomorphism, future research must investigate risks which may emerge from richer interaction with them. The impact of how an agent presents itself and its knowledge becomes greater.

papers.title: Measuring Human Resilience to Unreliable AI Assistance: A Stress-Test Framework for Human-AI Interaction
papers.abstract: As AI increasingly mediates human decisions, users must remain effective not only when assistance works as expected but also when its quality deteriorates. Human--AI research has developed rich measures of trust, reliance, and calibration, while human--autonomy research has examined resilience at the team and system levels. A missing measurement level is the human decision maker: how much task function is preserved or recovered when AI advice becomes unreliable?
